![](/static/base/1.0.1/images/icons/smileybones-small.svg)
![arXiv logo](/static/base/1.0.1/images/arxiv-logo-primary-light.svg)

# Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery

###### Abstract

Unsupervised skill discovery seeks to acquire different useful skills without extrinsic reward via unsupervised Reinforcement Learning (RL), with the discovered skills efficiently adapting to multiple downstream tasks in various ways. However, recent advanced skill discovery methods struggle to well balance state exploration and skill diversity, particularly when the potential skills are rich and hard to discern. In this paper, we propose Contrastive dynamic Skill Discovery (ComSD)11
1
Code and videos: https://github.com/liuxin0824/ComSD which generates diverse and exploratory unsupervised skills through a novel intrinsic incentive, named contrastive dynamic reward. It contains a particle-based exploration reward to make agents access far-reaching states for exploratory skill acquisition, and a novel contrastive diversity reward to promote the discriminability between different skills. Moreover, a novel dynamic weighting mechanism between the above two rewards is proposed to balance state exploration and skill diversity, which further enhances the quality of the discovered skills. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate that ComSD can generate diverse behaviors at different exploratory levels for multi-joint robots, enabling state-of-the-art adaptation performance on challenging downstream tasks. It can also discover distinguishable and far-reaching exploration skills in the challenging tree-like 2D maze.

###### Index Terms:

## I Introduction & Research Background

Under the supervision of extrinsic rewards, Reinforcement Learning (RL) enables agents to acquire effective task-specific skills  [[1](#bib.bib1), [2](#bib.bib2), [3](#bib.bib3)]. In contrast, however, real intelligent creatures, e.g., humans, are able to learn different useful task-agnostic skills without any supervision and utilize them to achieve multiple different tasks. To this end, unsupervised skill discovery is presented to simulate this process for machines [[4](#bib.bib4), [5](#bib.bib5), [6](#bib.bib6), [7](#bib.bib7)]. These approaches aim to generate various useful skills through training a skill-conditioned policy with a designed intrinsic reward, and the discovered skills can be utilized to efficiently achieve multiple downstream tasks in various ways, including skill finetuning, skill combination, and so on [[8](#bib.bib8)]. This necessitates (i) that the discovered skill set contains enough exploratory skills to ensure far-reaching exploration and state coverage (high state exploration) and (ii) that different skills corresponding to different skill condition vectors should be as different as possible (high skill diversity).

![Refer to caption](2309.17203v3/shiyitu-final.png)

Currently, many unsupervised skill discovery methods have shown promising results in different environments, such as goal-reaching robots [[7](#bib.bib7), [9](#bib.bib9), [10](#bib.bib10)] and maze exploration [[11](#bib.bib11), [12](#bib.bib12)]. The potential skill categories are relatively singular, and different skills are easily distinguishable in these domains. For more challenging benchmarks where the potential skills are rich and hard to distinguish by ending states, like URLB robot body movements [[13](#bib.bib13)], the skill discovery difficulty is dramatically increased (see Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction & Research Background ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery") left for a representative example). Recent advanced approaches cannot take both state exploration and skill diversity into account. For example, an ideal robot skill set should contain a variety of behaviors at different activity levels, while current advanced methods can either only learn different static postures (low state exploration) [[8](#bib.bib8), [14](#bib.bib14)] or only produce highly dynamic movements that are homogeneous (low skill diversity) [[15](#bib.bib15), [16](#bib.bib16)]. Some recent works have also noticed this issue [[11](#bib.bib11), [12](#bib.bib12)], but they only alleviate it on maze exploration problems and can’t well handle more challenging multi-joint robot behaviors. This is because their intrinsic rewards don’t provide effective incentives to seek and discern rich body movements for complex robots, and they also ignore the conflict between state exploration and skill diversity (see Section V-I) when potential skills are hard to discern by ending states.

In this paper, we propose Contrastive dynamic Skill Discovery (ComSD) which seeks exploratory and diverse unsupervised skills through a novel contrastive dynamic reward. It contains strong incentives to separately encourage skill diversity and state exploration through contrastive learning, with a novel dynamic weighting proposed for their balance. Concretely, this reward aims to maximize state-skill mutual information (MI), which is decomposed into skill-conditioned entropy (related to skill diversity) and state entropy (related to state exploration). For skill-conditioned entropy optimization, we conduct state-skill contrastive learning, utilizing the contrastive results as a novel diversity reward. For state entropy maximization, we employ a particle-based estimation as the exploration reward. With contrastive learning, the above rewards achieve accurate entropy estimation, thus providing effective encouragement. In domains with hard-to-discern skills, we observe a serious mutually exclusive effect between the above two entropy optimization processes (see Section IV-C). Thus, a Skill-based dynaMic Weighting (SMW) mechanism is proposed to weight the above rewards into our contrastive dynamic reward for balance between state exploration and skill diversity. We evaluate the adaptation ability of discovered robot behaviors on 16 skill combination downstream tasks and 16 skill finetuning downstream tasks (task details in Section III-A). ComSD enables state-of-the-art adaptation performance compared with five popular advanced methods, as shown in Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction & Research Background ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery") right. A detailed behavioral quality analysis is also provided, demonstrating that ComSD indeed generates qualified robot behaviors of both high state exploration and high skill diversity, which recent advanced methods cannot. ComSD can also discover distinguishable and far-reaching exploration skills in the challenging tree-like 2D maze.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

We propose Contrastive dynamic Skill Discovery (ComSD), a novel unsupervised skill discovery method, to generate exploratory and diverse unsupervised skills through a novel intrinsic incentive named contrastive dynamic reward. In this reward, we employ particle-based state entropy as an exploration reward for exploratory skill seeking, and propose to utilize the contrastive result between skill vectors and visited states as an explicit reward to promote diversity between different skills.

To alleviate the exploration hurt caused by explicitly employing the contrastive diversity reward, we propose a novel weighting mechanism, named SMW, that dynamically scales the exploration reward and the diversity reward based on skill vectors. SMW is the key to well balancing state exploration and skill diversity, further improving the quality of discovered unsupervised skills.

We conduct extensive numerical and analytical experiments. Results demonstrate that our proposed ComSD can discover diverse behaviors at different exploratory levels for challenging multi-joint robots, enabling state-of-the-art downstream adaptation ability on different kinds of downstream tasks. ComSD can also discover distinguishable and far-reaching exploration skills in the challenging tree-like 2D maze.

## II Related Works

Reinforcement Learning (RL) [[17](#bib.bib17), [18](#bib.bib18), [19](#bib.bib19)] has proven its effectiveness in learning useful task-specific skills in the presence of extrinsic rewards [[20](#bib.bib20), [21](#bib.bib21)]. The success of unsupervised learning in computer vision [[22](#bib.bib22)] and natural language processing [[23](#bib.bib23)] further benefits task-specific RL with visual input [[24](#bib.bib24), [25](#bib.bib25), [26](#bib.bib26)] by improving representation learning. However, the agents trained with lots of efforts are always hard to generalize their knowledge to novel tasks due to the task-specific supervision of extrinsic reward [[26](#bib.bib26)]. Inspired by the reward shaping approaches employed in inverse RL [[27](#bib.bib27), [28](#bib.bib28), [29](#bib.bib29)], unsupervised RL [[13](#bib.bib13)] is proposed to improve the multi-task generalization by designing task-agnostic rewards for unsupervised pre-training. The pre-trained feature encoders [[30](#bib.bib30), [31](#bib.bib31), [32](#bib.bib32)] and exploration policies [[33](#bib.bib33), [34](#bib.bib34), [35](#bib.bib35)] then can be implemented for efficient RL on different downstream tasks.
In addition to the generalization, intelligent agents should also be able to explore environments and learn different useful skills without any extrinsic supervision, like human beings. For the reasons above, unsupervised skill discovery [[4](#bib.bib4), [36](#bib.bib36)] is proposed and becomes a novel research hotspot. As a branch of unsupervised RL, unsupervised skill discovery also designs task-agnostic rewards and achieves unsupervised pre-training with these rewards, which guarantees task-agnostic downstream generalization[[37](#bib.bib37), [38](#bib.bib38)]. The main difference is that skill discovery requires extra input as conditions, named skill vectors. They aim to discover useful task-agnostic policies that are distinguishable by skill vectors. These approaches exhibit promising results across different fields [[39](#bib.bib39), [40](#bib.bib40), [41](#bib.bib41)]. However, in the URLB benchmark [[13](#bib.bib13)] where the potential skills are rich and hard to distinguish by ending states (discussion in Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction & Research Background ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery") left), it’s hard for current advanced MI-based methods [[15](#bib.bib15), [11](#bib.bib11), [12](#bib.bib12)] to take both state exploration and skill diversity into account. Recently, the distance-maximizing skill discovery methods [[7](#bib.bib7), [9](#bib.bib9), [10](#bib.bib10)] are proposed to discover diverse and far-reaching exploration skills for challenging goal-reaching tasks. However, these advanced goal-reaching skills are not very suitable for solving different types of the URLB downstream tasks that require different kinds of body movements [[12](#bib.bib12)]. In this paper, ComSD designs a dynamically weighted intrinsic incentive based on contrastive learning, discovering diverse robot behaviors at different exploratory levels in the URLB benchmark, which recent advanced methods cannot achieve.

## III Preliminaries

### III-A Problem Definition

Unsupervised skill discovery trains a skill-conditioned policy in a task-agnostic environment. Concretely, a reward-free Markov Decision Process (MDP) [[42](#bib.bib42)] is considered and defined as ℳf​r​e​e=(𝒮,𝒜,𝒫,γ,d0)\mathcal{M}^{free}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},\gamma,d\_{0}), where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the state space, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the action space, 𝒫\mathcal{P} is the distribution of the next state given the current state and action, γ\gamma is the discount factor, and d0d\_{0} is the distribution of the initial state. What skill discovery algorithms do is define an intrinsic reward ri​n​t​rr^{intr} and augment ℳf​r​e​e\mathcal{M}^{free} to an intrinsic-reward MDP ℳi​n​t​r=(𝒮,𝒜,𝒫,ri​n​t​r,γ,d0)\mathcal{M}^{intr}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},r^{intr},\gamma,d\_{0}). Then we denote the skill space by 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. With the skill vector zz (z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}) sampled from the skill distribution p⁡(z)p(z) defined by skill discovery algorithms, a skill-conditioned policy π⁡(a|s,z)\pi(a|s,z) can be obtained by RL over the ℳi​n​t​r\mathcal{M}^{intr}. We provide the pseudo-code of our ComSD in Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ IV-C Skill-based DynaMic Weighting (SMW) ‣ IV Unsupervised Skill Discovery by ComSD ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery") as a representative example to show the general pipeline of unsupervised skill discovery.

To evaluate the quality of discovered skills (i.e., the skill-conditioned agent π⁡(a|s,z)\pi(a|s,z)), two adaptation evaluations: skill combination and skill finetuning are employed on each task-specific downstream task. A downstream task can be described as an extrinsic-reward MDP ℳe​x​t​r=(𝒮,𝒜,𝒫,re​x​t​r,γ,d0)\mathcal{M}^{extr}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},r^{extr},\gamma,d\_{0}), where re​x​t​rr^{extr} denotes the task-specific extrinsic reward. In skill combination, the learned π⁡(a|s,z)\pi(a|s,z) is frozen, and a meta-controller π′​(z|s)\pi^{\prime}(z|s) is required to choose and combine skill vectors for π⁡(a|s,z)\pi(a|s,z) automatically on downstream tasks. Concretely, over the original downstream task ℳe​x​t​r\mathcal{M}^{extr}, skill combination can be defined as ℳe​x​t​r′=(𝒮,𝒵,𝒫′,re​x​t​r′,γ,d0)\mathcal{M}^{extr^{\prime}}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{Z},\mathcal{P^{\prime}},r^{extr^{\prime}},\gamma,d\_{0}), which regards different skill vectors z∼𝒵z\sim\mathcal{Z} as its actions and correspondingly changes its transition model and reward function. The meta-controller π′​(z|s)\pi^{\prime}(z|s) is trained over ℳe​x​t​r′\mathcal{M}^{extr^{\prime}} by RL and then used for evaluation of the learned π⁡(a|s,z)\pi(a|s,z). In skill finetuning, a target skill vector ziz\_{i} is chosen. The corresponding policy π⁡(a|s,zi)\pi(a|s,z\_{i}) is further finetuned on the ℳe​x​t​r\mathcal{M}^{extr} for a few steps and serves as the evaluation of the discovered π⁡(a|s,z)\pi(a|s,z). The pseudo-codes of two adaptation evaluations are provided in Algorithm [2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ V-B Baselines ‣ V Experiments & Analysis ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery") and Algorithm [3](#alg3 "Algorithm 3 ‣ V-D Skill Finetuning ‣ V Experiments & Analysis ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery") respectively (Section V).

### III-B Mutual Information Objective of Unsupervised RL

As current state-of-the-art approaches do [[15](#bib.bib15), [14](#bib.bib14), [8](#bib.bib8)], our ComSD tries to maximize the Mutual Information (MI) objective between state function τ\tau and skill vector zz for behavior discovery. τ\tau is defined as state transitions (τ=concat⁡(st−1,st)\tau={\rm concat}(s^{t-1},s^{t}))
throughout this paper. The MI objective I⁡(τ,z)I(\tau;z) can be decomposed into the form of Shannon entropy in two ways:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | I⁡(τ,z)=−H⁡(z|τ)+H⁡(z),I(\tau;z)=-H(z|\tau)+H(z), |  | (1) |

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | I⁡(τ,z)=−H⁡(τ|z)+H⁡(τ),I(\tau;z)=-H(\tau|z)+H(\tau), |  | (2) |

where the I⁡(⋅,⋅)I(\cdot;\cdot) denotes the MI function and H⁡(⋅)H(\cdot) denotes the Shannon entropy throughout the paper. Most classical MI-based algorithms [[43](#bib.bib43), [8](#bib.bib8), [16](#bib.bib16)] are based on the first decomposition Eq. ([1](#S3.E1 "In III-B Mutual Information Objective of Unsupervised RL ‣ III Preliminaries ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery")). A uniform random policy can guarantee the maximum of the skill entropy H⁡(z)H(z) while the trainable discriminators estimating the state-conditioned entropy H⁡(z|τ)H(z|\tau) are employed as the intrinsic rewards for unsupervised RL. However,  [[13](#bib.bib13), [15](#bib.bib15)] have found it hard for these methods to guarantee robot state exploration without any external balancing signals. To this end, some recent works [[44](#bib.bib44), [14](#bib.bib14), [15](#bib.bib15)] focus on the second decomposition Eq. ([2](#S3.E2 "In III-B Mutual Information Objective of Unsupervised RL ‣ III Preliminaries ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery")) to explicitly optimize the state entropy H⁡(τ)H(\tau) by designing exploration rewards, achieving considerable performance in different domains, including robotic manipulation, video games, and challenging robot locomotion. Following these, we choose Eq. ([2](#S3.E2 "In III-B Mutual Information Objective of Unsupervised RL ‣ III Preliminaries ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery")) as our optimization target.

## IV Unsupervised Skill Discovery by ComSD

In this section, we show how ComSD seeks skills of both skill diversity and state exploration via a novel contrastive dynamic reward rC​o​m​S​Di​n​t​rr^{intr}\_{ComSD} based on Eq. ([2](#S3.E2 "In III-B Mutual Information Objective of Unsupervised RL ‣ III Preliminaries ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery")). In Section IV-A, we propose a novel diversity reward rc​o​n​t​r​a​s​td​i​v​e​r​s​i​t​yr^{diversity}\_{contrast} through contrastive learning to estimate the skill-conditioned entropy. In Section IV-B, we illustrate the way to estimate the state entropy by a particle-based exploration reward re​x​p​l​o​r​a​t​i​o​nr^{exploration}. In Section IV-C, we detail why and how to balance the above two rewards into our contrastive dynamic reward with the proposed SMW. The overall design of our proposed contrastive dynamic reward rC​o​m​S​Di​n​t​rr^{intr}\_{ComSD} is shown in Fig. [3](#S4.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ IV Unsupervised Skill Discovery by ComSD ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery").

### IV-A Skill-conditioned Entropy Estimation via Contrastive Learning

In decomposition Eq. ([2](#S3.E2 "In III-B Mutual Information Objective of Unsupervised RL ‣ III Preliminaries ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery")), higher negative conditioned entropy −H⁡(τ|z)-H(\tau|z) means lower state coverage within each skill. When the overall exploration of all skills, i.e., state entropy H⁡(τ)H(\tau), is guaranteed (discussed in Section IV-B), increasing −H⁡(τ|z)-H(\tau|z) reduces exploration within each skill, forcing the agent to exploit skill-specific information and maintain unique information for different skills, i.e., increasing the diversity of learned skills. We provide an example to illustrate this process, as shown in Fig. [2](#S3.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ III-B Mutual Information Objective of Unsupervised RL ‣ III Preliminaries ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery").

Due to the unavailable conditioned distribution, we can’t directly maximize the −H⁡(τ|z)-H(\tau|z) but try to maximize its lower bound. First, −H⁡(τ|z)-H(\tau|z) can be decomposed as:

|  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | −H⁡(τ|z)\displaystyle-H(\tau|z) | =∑τ,zp⁡(τ,z)​log⁡p⁡(τ|z)\displaystyle=\sum\_{\tau,z}p(\tau,z)\log p(\tau|z) |  | (3) |
|  |  | =∑τ,zp⁡(τ,z)​log⁡p⁡(τ,z)p⁡(z)\displaystyle=\sum\_{\tau,z}p(\tau,z)\log\frac{p(\tau,z)}{p(z)} |  |
|  |  | =∑τ,zp⁡(τ,z)​(log⁡p⁡(τ,z)−log⁡p⁡(z)),\displaystyle=\sum\_{\tau,z}p(\tau,z)(\log p(\tau,z)-\log p(z)), |  |

where p⁡(⋅)p(\cdot) denotes probability throughout the paper. Following previous works [[11](#bib.bib11), [15](#bib.bib15)], we use a uniform distribution to generate the skill vectors. Therefore, the term log​p​(z)\rm log\it p(z) becomes a constant, and we denote it as cc:

|  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | −H⁡(τ|z)\displaystyle-H(\tau|z) | =∑τ,zp⁡(τ,z)​(log​p​(τ,z)−c)\displaystyle=\sum\_{\tau,z}p(\tau,z)(\rm log\it p(\tau,z)-c) |  | (4) |
|  |  | =∑τ,zp⁡(τ,z)​log​p​(τ,z)−∑τ,zp⁡(τ,z)⋅c\displaystyle=\sum\_{\tau,z}p(\tau,z)\rm log\it p(\tau,z)-\sum\_{\tau,z}p(\tau,z)\cdot c |  |
|  |  | =∑τ,zp⁡(τ,z)​l​o​g​p​(τ,z)−c.\displaystyle=\sum\_{\tau,z}p(\tau,z)logp(\tau,z)-c. |  |

We neglect cc and then obtain the variational lower bound:

|  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | −H′​(τ|z)\displaystyle-H^{\prime}(\tau|z) | =∑τ,zp⁡(τ,z)​log⁡p⁡(τ,z)\displaystyle=\sum\_{\tau,z}p(\tau,z)\log p(\tau,z) |  | (5) |
|  |  | =∑τ,zp⁡(τ,z)​log⁡p⁡(τ,z)\displaystyle=\sum\_{\tau,z}p(\tau,z)\log p(\tau,z) |  |
|  |  | +∑τ,zp(τ,z)logq(τ,z)−∑τ,zp(τ,z)logq(τ,z)\displaystyle+\sum\_{\tau,z}p(\tau,z)\log q(\tau,z)-\sum\_{\tau,z}p(\tau,z)\log q(\tau,z) |  |
|  |  | =∑τ,zp(τ,z)logq(τ,z)+DKL(p(τ,z)||q(τ,z))\displaystyle=\sum\_{\tau,z}p(\tau,z)\log q(\tau,z)+D\_{\rm KL}(p(\tau,z)||q(\tau,z)) |  |
|  |  | =𝔼τ,z[logq(τ,z)]+DKL(p(τ,z)||q(τ,z))\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\_{\tau,z}[\log q(\tau,z)]+D\_{\rm KL}(p(\tau,z)||q(\tau,z)) |  |
|  |  | ≥𝔼τ,z​[log⁡q⁡(τ,z)],\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}\_{\tau,z}[\log q(\tau,z)], |  |

where q⁡(τ,z)q(\tau,z) is employed to estimate the unavailable p⁡(τ,z)p(\tau,z). To optimize −H⁡(τ|z)-H(\tau|z), we need to minimize the KL divergence DKL(p(τ,z)||q(τ,z))D\_{\rm KL}(p(\tau,z)||q(\tau,z)) and maximize the expectation 𝔼τ,z​[log⁡q⁡(τ,z)]\mathbb{E}\_{\tau,z}[\log q(\tau,z)].

For KL divergence minimization, the distribution qq should be as positively correlated with the probability function pp as possible. We define qq as the exponential inner product between the state embeddings and skill embeddings:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | q⁡(τ,z)=exp⁡fθ1​(τ)⋅fθ2​(z)‖fθ1​(τ)‖⋅‖fθ2​(z)‖​T,q(\tau,z)=\exp\frac{f\_{\theta\_{1}}(\tau)\cdot f\_{\theta\_{2}}(z)}{||f\_{\theta\_{1}}(\tau)||\cdot||f\_{\theta\_{2}}(z)||T}, |  | (6) |

where fθ1​(⋅)f\_{\theta\_{1}}(\cdot) is the state encoder, fθ2​(⋅)f\_{\theta\_{2}}(\cdot) is the skill encoder, TT is the temperature parameter, and exp⁡(⋅)\exp(\cdot) makes qq non-negative like pp. The above two encoders are updated by gradient descent after computing the NCE loss [[45](#bib.bib45)] in contrastive learning [[22](#bib.bib22)]:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

### IV-C Skill-based DynaMic Weighting (SMW)

With the negative conditioned entropy −H⁡(τ|z)-H(\tau|z) estimated by rc​o​n​t​r​a​s​td​i​v​e​r​s​i​t​yr^{diversity}\_{contrast} and the state entropy estimated by re​x​p​l​o​r​a​t​i​o​nr^{exploration}, a naive way for intrinsic reward design is to employ a fixed coefficient α\alpha to scale the two terms (ri​n​t​r=re​x​p​l​o​r​a​t​i​o​n+α⋅rc​o​n​t​r​a​s​td​i​v​e​r​s​i​t​yr^{intr}=r^{exploration}+\alpha\cdot r^{diversity}\_{contrast}). However, in practice, we find it impossible to use a fixed coefficient to balance them well when potential skills are rich, hard to explore, and hard to distinguish by only ending states. Concretely, when employing re​x​p​l​o​r​a​t​i​o​nr^{exploration} alone, the robots can only learn dynamic movements of high activity but not other exploratory levels, and the learned behaviors are highly homogeneous (high exploration but low exploitation). Increasing the fixed weight α\alpha of rc​o​n​t​r​a​s​td​i​v​e​r​s​i​t​yr^{diversity}\_{contrast} can surely improve the skill diversity, but it will simultaneously reduce the state exploration (see experiments in Section V-I), making robots prefer static postures (easily distinguished by simple ending states) but ignore active movements (distinguished by trajectories but not only ending states). The large fixed weight leads to high exploitation but low exploration. This is because distilling ending states into skill vectors is an easy-to-reach local optimal solution for state-skill MI maximization. In addition, this conflict between exploration and diversity also exists in other advanced methods (Section V-I).

We propose Skill-based dynaMic Weighting (SMW), an easy-but-effective weighting mechanism to mitigate the issue above. The main idea of SMW is to set different learning objectives for different skills instead of using fixed learning objectives across all skills. Concretely, it designs another changeable coefficient β⁡(z)\beta(z) which is dynamically adjusted according to skill vectors. β⁡(z)\beta(z) is defined as:

|  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | β⁡(z)=clamp⁡(β′,(wℎ𝑖𝑔ℎ,w𝑙𝑜𝑤)),\displaystyle\beta(z)=\rm clamp\it(\beta^{\prime},(w\_{high},w\_{low})), |  | (11) |
|  | w​h​e​r​eβ′\displaystyle where\ \ \beta^{\prime} | =(wh​i​g​h−wl​o​wfh​i​g​h−fl​o​w)​(flag⁡(z)−fℎ𝑖𝑔ℎ)+wℎ𝑖𝑔ℎ.\displaystyle=(\frac{w\_{high}-w\_{low}}{f\_{high}-f\_{low}})(\rm flag\it(z)-f\_{high})+w\_{high}. |  |

The flag⁡(⋅)\rm flag\it(\cdot) is a function to map the high-dimensional skill vectors into 1-dimensional flag variables. Here, we find that naively employing the first dimension of skill vectors as the flag variables (i.e., flag⁡(z)=I1T⋅z,where​I1=(1,0,…,0)\rm flag\it(z)=I\_{1}^{T}\cdot z,\ {\rm where}\ I\_{1}=(1,0,...,0)) enables considerable results in practice. The fixed hyper-parameters wh​i​g​h,wl​o​w,fh​i​g​h,fl​o​ww\_{high},w\_{low},f\_{high},f\_{low} and the clamp function clamp⁡(⋅)\rm clamp\it(\cdot) make the dynamic coefficient β\beta linearly related to flag variables flag⁡(z)\rm flag\it(z) with different slopes in different regions. We clearly visualize the relation between β\beta and flag⁡(z)\rm flag\it(z) in Fig. [3](#S4.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ IV Unsupervised Skill Discovery by ComSD ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery") right. With SMW, the skill space is actually divided into different regions with different learning objectives. In the high-exploration region (flag⁡(z)<f𝑙𝑜𝑤\rm flag\it(z)<f\_{low}, corresponding to low diversity reward weight), the agents try their best to explore, while in the high-exploitation region (flag⁡(z)>fℎ𝑖𝑔ℎ\rm flag\it(z)>f\_{high}, corresponding to high diversity reward weight), the agents pay more attention to discerning learned skills. In the middle (flag⁡(z)\rm flag\it(z) between fl​o​wf\_{low} and fh​i​g​hf\_{high}), the agents can acquire behaviors at different activity levels (corresponding to different β\beta values). The contrastive dynamic reward of ComSD is defined as:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | rC​o​m​S​Di​n​t​r=re​x​p​l​o​r​a​t​i​o​n+α⋅β⁡(z)⋅rc​o​n​t​r​a​s​td​i​v​e​r​s​i​t​y.r^{intr}\_{ComSD}=r^{exploration}+\alpha\cdot\beta(z)\cdot r^{diversity}\_{contrast}. |  | (12) |

Over the intrinsic-reward MDP ℳi​n​t​r\mathcal{M}^{intr} augmented by rC​o​m​S​Di​n​t​rr^{intr}\_{ComSD}, ComSD trains the skill-conditioned policy π⁡(a|s,z)\pi(a|s,z) via RL with zz sampled by uniform distribution. Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ IV-C Skill-based DynaMic Weighting (SMW) ‣ IV Unsupervised Skill Discovery by ComSD ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery") provides the full pseudo-code of ComSD.

## V Experiments & Analysis

### V-A Environments

On the importance of environments: OpenAI Gym [[39](#bib.bib39)] and DMC [[47](#bib.bib47)] are two of the most popular continuous robot locomotion benchmarks. In Gym, the episode ends when agents lose their balance, while the episode length in DMC is fixed. [[15](#bib.bib15)] found this small difference makes DMC much harder for reward-free exploration, and most classical methods succeeding in OpenAI Gym suffer from lazy exploration in DMC. This is mainly because the agents have to learn balance by themselves without any external signals in DMC. To this end, we employ the challenging DMC [[47](#bib.bib47)] and URLB [[13](#bib.bib13)] (the most popular skill discovery benchmark based on DMC) as our environments.

Following recent advanced methods [[15](#bib.bib15), [31](#bib.bib31), [32](#bib.bib32), [24](#bib.bib24), [26](#bib.bib26), [25](#bib.bib25)], we employ 16 downstream tasks of 4 domains from URLB [[13](#bib.bib13)] and DMC [[47](#bib.bib47)] for skill adaptation evaluation. The domains Walker, Quadruped, Cheetah, and Hopper are recognized as the most representative and challenging multi-joint robot environments, each of which contains 4 totally diverse and challenging downstream tasks.

In each domain, all the methods pre-train their agents for 2M environment steps with their respective intrinsic rewards, which follows previous works [[15](#bib.bib15), [11](#bib.bib11)]. The hyper-parameters of all baselines follow the official implementations [[13](#bib.bib13)] and we provide the detailed settings of ComSD in Table [IV](#S6.T4 "TABLE IV ‣ VI Conclusion & Limitation ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery"). After unsupervised pre-training, the discovered skills will be fully evaluated on two adaptation evaluations: skill combination [[8](#bib.bib8)] and skill combination in URLB [[13](#bib.bib13)] respectively, across all 16 downstream tasks with extrinsic reward. It means a total of 32 numerical results are employed for one method’s evaluation. DDPG [[48](#bib.bib48)] is chosen as the backbone RL algorithm for all methods throughout the paper. The detailed settings of the skill combination and skill finetuning are provided along with the experimental results.

Following recent advanced works [[11](#bib.bib11), [12](#bib.bib12)], we also conduct experiments on 2D maze exploration [[41](#bib.bib41)], where an agent is required to explore the different parts under different skills and maximize its whole exploration in the maze. Different skills can be well represented by the sampled trajectories that can be easily visualized by different colors. We choose the challenging tree-like maze, which consists of two branches and four leaves. See Section V-K for concrete maze structure. The environment settings all follow previous works [[11](#bib.bib11), [12](#bib.bib12)].

### V-B Baselines

We compare our ComSD with six recent advanced algorithms: CeSD [[12](#bib.bib12)], BeCL [[11](#bib.bib11)], CIC [[15](#bib.bib15)], APS [[14](#bib.bib14)], SMM [[16](#bib.bib16)], and DIAYN [[8](#bib.bib8)]. These advanced methods are currently state-of-the-art for challenging robot behavior discovery [[13](#bib.bib13)] and maze exploration [[41](#bib.bib41)].

DIAYN [[8](#bib.bib8)] is one of the most classical and original unsupervised skill discovery algorithms, proposing to maximize the MI between skills and states. It employs the first MI decomposition, Eq. ([1](#S3.E1 "In III-B Mutual Information Objective of Unsupervised RL ‣ III Preliminaries ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery")). It uses a discrete uniform prior distribution to guarantee the maximization of skill entropy H⁡(z)H(z). The negative state-conditioned entropy −H⁡(z|s)-H(z|s) is estimated by a trainable discriminator log​p​(z|s){\rm log}p(z|s) which computes the intrinsic reward. As a foundational work, it provides several reasonable evaluations of skill adaptation, of which skill finetuning and skill combination are employed in our experiments.

SMM [[16](#bib.bib16)] aims to learn a policy for which the state marginal distribution matches a given target state distribution. It optimizes the objective by reducing it to a two-player, zero-sum game between a state density model and a parametric policy. Like DIAYN, it is also based on the first decomposition Eq. ([1](#S3.E1 "In III-B Mutual Information Objective of Unsupervised RL ‣ III Preliminaries ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery")) of the MI objective.

Require: Reward-specific environment EsE\_{s}, the pre-trained skill-conditioned policy π⁡(a|s,z)\pi(a|s,z), environment adaption steps IaI\_{a}, and the RL batch size IbI\_{b}.

Initialize: The meta-controller (actor) π′​(z|s)\pi^{\prime}(z|s), the critic Q⁡(z,s)Q(z,s), and the replay buffer DD.

Output: The performance of π′​(z|s)\pi^{\prime}(z|s) serves as the skill combination evaluation result.

APS [[14](#bib.bib14)] employs the second decomposition Eq. ([2](#S3.E2 "In III-B Mutual Information Objective of Unsupervised RL ‣ III Preliminaries ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery")) for its MI estimation. For state entropy estimation, it employs a popular particle-based entropy estimation proposed by APT [[30](#bib.bib30)] for exploration. For skill-conditioned entropy, it chooses the successor feature [[49](#bib.bib49)] as a diversity reward with a fixed weight. APS achieves considerable results on video games [[40](#bib.bib40)] but can’t provide enough incentives for robots, suffering from lazy exploration [[15](#bib.bib15)].

CIC [[15](#bib.bib15)] is a state-of-the-art robot behavior discovery method on URLB. It first introduces contrastive learning [[22](#bib.bib22)] into unsupervised skill discovery. It chooses the second MI decomposition, Eq. ([2](#S3.E2 "In III-B Mutual Information Objective of Unsupervised RL ‣ III Preliminaries ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery")) with APT particle-based estimation for state entropy estimation, like APS. The contrastive learning between state transitions and skill vectors is conducted for implicit skill-conditioned entropy maximization. We find that the robot behaviors produced by CIC are of high activity but low skill diversity.

BeCL [[11](#bib.bib11)] is another state-of-the-art method on URLB [[13](#bib.bib13)] and maze exploration [[41](#bib.bib41)]. It tries to mitigate the diversity problem in CIC by designing a novel MI objective, I⁡(s1,s2)I(s^{1},s^{2}), where s1s^{1} and s2s^{2} denote different states generated by the same skill. BeCL can’t generate enough dynamic robot behaviors, and their intrinsic reward computational consumption is also much larger than other approaches.

CeSD [[12](#bib.bib12)] uses an ensemble of skills for partitioned exploration based on state prototypes, enabling local exploration within clusters while maximizing overall state coverage. It also employs the second decomposition Eq. ([2](#S3.E2 "In III-B Mutual Information Objective of Unsupervised RL ‣ III Preliminaries ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery")) for MI estimation. It achieves advanced results across both robot locomotion [[13](#bib.bib13)] and maze explorations [[41](#bib.bib41)].

The close baselines to our ComSD are CIC and APS, where they all design intrinsic rewards based on Eq. ([2](#S3.E2 "In III-B Mutual Information Objective of Unsupervised RL ‣ III Preliminaries ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery")). Apart from the most notable difference, a novel weighting mechanism (SMW), ComSD still significantly differs from these methods. CIC doesn’t design a diversity incentive, while ComSD proposes a novel contrastive diversity reward to explicitly encourage diversity. APS also employs both diversity reward and exploration reward, but it doesn’t conduct contrastive learning that is the key to providing effective and strong incentives for challenging robots. In addition, BeCL also employs contrastive learning, but their contrastive components are different states generated by the same skill, which differs from ours.

### V-C Skill Combination

In skill combination evaluation [[8](#bib.bib8)], another meta-controller π′​(z|s)\pi^{\prime}(z|s) which selects the discovered skills automatically to achieve downstream tasks, is trained. The discovered skill-conditioned agent π⁡(a|s,z)\pi(a|s,z) is frozen, and π′​(z|s)\pi^{\prime}(z|s) is trained by RL with extrinsic reward (concrete process is provided in Algorithm [2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ V-B Baselines ‣ V Experiments & Analysis ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery")). As it doesn’t allow for adjustments to learned skills with real reward, skill combination is very challenging for unsupervised skill discovery methods, requiring both state exploration and skill diversity. It is one of the most comprehensive skill quality evaluations. For each method, 2M environment steps RL are allowed to train their meta-controllers. All the hyper-parameters are shared across all the methods for a fair comparison, which we detail in Table [IV](#S6.T4 "TABLE IV ‣ VI Conclusion & Limitation ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery"). The results of ComSD are obtained over six different random seeds.

The training curves for 16 skill combination downstream tasks are shown in Fig. [4](#S5.F4 "Fig. 4 ‣ V-B Baselines ‣ V Experiments & Analysis ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery"), where the solid line represents the mean and the shade denotes the standard deviation. DIAYN, SMM, and BeCL cannot obtain effective policies in most downstream tasks (e.g., they all fail in Hopper). CeSD achieves considerable results on Quadruped tasks but fails in the others. These phenomena fully confirm the difficulty of this benchmark for skill discovery methods. In this situation, ComSD enables effective policy learning and outperforms all 6 baselines across 15/16 downstream tasks, demonstrating that the robot behaviors discovered by ComSD are of much higher quality (both state exploration and skill diversity) than all other methods. CIC and APS are the two most competitive baselines. Both of them and our ComSD employ the decomposition Eq. ([2](#S3.E2 "In III-B Mutual Information Objective of Unsupervised RL ‣ III Preliminaries ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery")), which indicates the importance of explicitly maximizing exploration. An interesting phenomenon is that CIC always gets a higher initial score than APS and ComSD but has no upward trend, which coincides with the fact that CIC can only produce exploratory but homogeneous behaviors (skill visualization in Section V-J). The results will be similar no matter how these homogeneous skills are combined by the meta-controller. By contrast, APS and ComSD explicitly maximize the conditioned entropy through diversity reward, greatly improving the diversity of learned skill sets and achieving higher final scores than CIC. Compared with APS, ComSD performs better due to the following two reasons: First, the contrastive learning employed by ComSD provides stronger incentives for exploration and exploitation in challenging robot domains. Second, the proposed SMW enables ComSD to learn diverse behaviors at different activity levels, thus gaining better adaptation to both static and dynamic downstream tasks.

### V-D Skill Finetuning

In skill finetuning evaluation [[13](#bib.bib13)], a skill vector ziz\_{i} is chosen, and the corresponding skill π(⋅|s,zi)\pi(\cdot|s,z\_{i}) is finetuned with the extrinsic reward (concrete process is provided in Algorithm [3](#alg3 "Algorithm 3 ‣ V-D Skill Finetuning ‣ V Experiments & Analysis ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery")). Since reward-specific skill adjustments are allowed, this adaptation is much easier than skill combination. 100k environment steps with extrinsic reward are allowed for each method, where one skill is selected in the first 4k steps and then finetuned in another 96k steps. For skill selection, previous works employ random sampling [[11](#bib.bib11)], fixed choice [[15](#bib.bib15)], or reward-based choice [[14](#bib.bib14)]. We follow the official implementation of  [[15](#bib.bib15)], employing a fixed mean value (0.5) for all dimensions of the skill vector except the first. We set the first dimension to 00, because when the first skill dimension (flag variable) is set to 0 (lower than fl​o​wf\_{low}), the skills have high exploration (see Section IV-C), achieving better results. All the hyper-parameters are shared across different methods for a fair comparison. We show the detailed experimental settings in Table [IV](#S6.T4 "TABLE IV ‣ VI Conclusion & Limitation ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery"). The results of ComSD are obtained over ten different seeds.

Require: Reward-specific environment EsE\_{s}, the pre-trained skill-conditioned policy π⁡(a|s,z)\pi(a|s,z), environment adaption steps IaI\_{a}, the RL batch size IbI\_{b}, and skill choice steps IcI\_{c}.

Initialize: The critic Q⁡(a,c​o​n​c​a​t​(s,z))Q(a,concat(s,z)) and replay buffer DD.

Output: The performance of π⁡(a|s,zi)\pi(a|s,z\_{i}) serves as the skill finetuning evaluation result.

The numerical results on 16 downstream tasks are shown in Table [I](#S5.T1 "TABLE I ‣ V-B Baselines ‣ V Experiments & Analysis ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery"), where the first value represents the mean and the second value denotes the standard deviation. CeSD, CIC, and BeCL are current state-of-the-art methods in URLB skill finetuning. Compared with CIC and BeCL, ComSD performs comparably or better on 11 and 12 downstream tasks, respectively. It also obtains competitive or higher scores than CeSD on 11 downstream tasks. These demonstrate that ComSD achieves competitive performance with current state-of-the-art methods. Actually, the score of the initial few steps has little to do with the final score in state-based locomotion. It’s hard to find a proper skill from a large skill set within only 4K steps. This explains why CIC, BeCL, CeSD, and our ComSD use random or fixed skill choices to achieve the advanced performance. Meanwhile, it means this evaluation does not adequately judge the skill diversity (only one skill is employed for evaluation), and is even less favorable to a more diverse skill set, because higher skill diversity causes higher skill choice difficulties. In this situation, ComSD discovers the most diverse robot behaviors (see skill combination in Section V-C and diversity analysis in Section V-G&H) while simultaneously achieving competitive performance on skill finetuning, which further shows its superior behavioral quality.

### V-E Adaptation Ablation

We conduct adaptation ablation experiments to show the effectiveness of (i) the contrastive diversity reward rc​o​n​t​r​a​s​td​i​v​e​r​s​i​t​yr^{diversity}\_{contrast} and (ii) the skill-based dynamic weighting (SMW) mechanism in Fig. [5](#S5.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ V-D Skill Finetuning ‣ V Experiments & Analysis ‣ Balancing State Exploration and Skill Diversity in Unsupervised Skill Discovery"). ’ComSD w/o SMW’ denotes ablating the SMW, i.e., removing the dynamic weight β⁡(z)\beta(z) in Eq. (12). ’ComSD w/o SMW&rc​o​n​t​r​a​s​td​i​v​e​r​s​i​t​yr^{diversity}\_{contrast}’ denotes removing the contrastive diversity reward, i.e., only employing the exploration reward re​x​p​l​o​r​a​t​i​o​nr^{exploration}. ’ComSD w/o SMW&CL’ denotes that based on ’ComSD w/o SMW’, Contrastive Learning (CL) is further removed, which is actually APS [[14](#bib.bib14)]. Ċompared with no diversity reward (’ComSD w/o SMW&rc​o​n​t​r​a​s​td​i​v​e​r​s​i​t​yr^{diversity}\_{contrast}’), designing a concrete diversity reward (’ComSD w/o SMW&CL’ and ’ComSD w/o SMW’) enables better skill diversity, which corresponds to the larger curve slope in skill combination. Moreover, contrastive learning enables better performance on both kinds of adaptations. In practice, a fixed diversity reward coefficient (’ComSD w/o SMW&CL’ and ’ComSD w/o SMW’) cannot provide a balance between state exploration and skill diversity. The direct intervention of diversity reward indeed improves diversity but simultaneously reduces exploration (more details in Section V-I), causing huge performance drops in skill finetuning. The proposed SMW enables agents to balance them well, effectively alleviating the state exploration decline and corresponding performance drops in skill finetuning. In summary, both rc​o​n​t​r​a​s​td​i​v​e​r​s​i​t​yr^{diversity}\_{contrast} and SMW are necessary in ComSD.

### V-F Hyper-parameter Sensitivity

In this section, we provide the hyper-parameter selecting process (i.e., sensitivity analysis) of SMW. args.key_excerpts: We propose Contrastive dynamic Skill Discovery (ComSD) which generates diverse and exploratory unsupervised skills through a novel intrinsic incentive, named contrastive dynamic reward.,ComSD enables state-of-the-art adaptation performance compared with five popular advanced methods...,We propose a novel weighting mechanism, named SMW, that dynamically scales the exploration reward and the diversity reward based on skill vectors.,SMW is the key to well balancing state exploration and skill diversity, further improving the quality of discovered unsupervised skills.,ComSD outperforms all 6 baselines across 15/16 downstream tasks, demonstrating that the robot behaviors discovered by ComSD are of much higher quality (both state exploration and skill diversity) than all other methods.
args.summary: This paper presents Contrastive dynamic Skill Discovery (ComSD), a novel unsupervised skill discovery method for reinforcement learning that balances state exploration and skill diversity. The key challenge addressed is that existing methods either produce diverse but static skills (low exploration) or dynamic but homogeneous skills (low diversity). ComSD introduces a contrastive dynamic reward composed of: (1) a particle-based exploration reward to encourage far-reaching state exploration, (2) a contrastive diversity reward that uses state-skill contrastive learning to maximize discriminability between different skills, and (3) a Skill-based dynaMic Weighting (SMW) mechanism that dynamically adjusts the balance between exploration and diversity rewards based on skill vectors. This allows different skills to have different learning objectives — some focused on exploration, others on exploitation. Experiments on the URLB benchmark (Walker, Quadruped, Cheetah, Hopper domains) and a 2D tree-like maze demonstrate that ComSD achieves state-of-the-art performance on 15/16 skill combination downstream tasks and competitive performance on skill finetuning compared to six baselines (DIAYN, SMM, APS, CIC, BeCL, CeSD). The method generates diverse robot behaviors at different activity levels, enabling superior adaptation to downstream tasks.

You are tasked with summarizing the raw content of a webpage retrieved from a web search. Your goal is to create a summary that preserves the most important information from the original web page.
