We hypothesize that this discrepancy is due to the difficulty of fitting the conditional log-partition function estimator, which is required for the TB objective but not for VarGrad, which only learns the policy. (In Fig. D.1 we show decoded samples encoded using the best-performing diffusion encoder.) 9 5.3 Extensions to general SDE learning problems Our implementation of diffusion-structured generative flow networks includes several additional options that diverge from the modeling assumptions made in most past work in the field. Notably, it features the ability to: • optimize the backward (noising) process – not only the denoising process – as was done for related learning problems in [12, 63, 79]; • learn the forward process’s diffusion rate 𝑔(x𝑡, 𝑡; 𝜃), not only the mean 𝑢(x𝑡, 𝑡; 𝜃); • assume a varying noise schedule for the backward process, making it possible to train models with standard noising SDEs used for diffusion models for images.
These extensions will allow others to build on our implementation and apply it to problems such as finetuning diffusion models trained on images with a GFlowNet objective.
As noted in §5.1, in the main experiments we fixed the diffusion rate of the learned forward process, an assumption inherited from all past work and justified in the continuous-time limit. However, we perform an experiment to show the importance of extensions such as learning the forward variance in discrete time. Fig. 3 shows the samples of models on the 25GMM energy following the experimental setup of [43]. We see that when the forward policy’s variance is learned, the model can better capture the details of the target distributions, choosing a low variance in the vicinity of the peaks to avoid ‘blurring’ them through the noise added in the last step of sampling.
In §C.2, we include preliminary results using a variance-preserving backward process, as commonly used in diffusion models, in place of the reversed Brownian motion used in the main experiments.
The ability to model distributions accurately in fewer steps is important for computational efficiency.
Future work can consider ways to improve performance in coarse time discretizations, such as non-Gaussian transitions, whose utility in diffusion models trained from data has been demonstrated [82].
6 Conclusion We have presented a study of diffusion-structured samplers for amortized inference over continuous variables. Our results suggest promising techniques for improving the mode coverage and efficiency of these models. Future work on applications can consider inference of high-dimensional parameters of dynamical systems and inverse problems. In probabilistic machine learning, extensions of this work should study integration of our amortized sequential samplers as variational posteriors in an expectation-maximization loop for training latent variable models, as was recently done for discrete compositional latents by [33], and for sampling Bayesian posteriors over high-dimensional model parameters. The most important direction of theoretical work is understanding the continuous-time limit (𝑇→∞) of all the algorithms we have studied.
Note added in final version: In a paper that appeared subsequently to the publication of this work, Berner et al. [9] have shown connections among the families of diffusion sampling algorithms considered here and analyzed their continuous-time limits.

args.summary:
This paper (NeurIPS 2024) studies training diffusion models to sample from unnormalized probability densities (energy functions). The authors benchmark several diffusion-structured inference methods, including simulation-based variational approaches (PIS, DDS, DIS) and off-policy methods (continuous GFlowNets). They introduce a unified library for diffusion-structured samplers to address reproducibility issues in prior work.

**Key contributions:**
1. **Unified benchmarking library** - Enables fair comparison of methods under consistent conditions, calling into question some prior claims about robustness and sample efficiency.

2. **Exploration and credit assignment techniques:**
   - Subtrajectory balance (SubTB) with partial energies offers little benefit over trajectory balance (TB) in the diffusion setting
   - Langevin parametrization (LP) - incorporating gradient information into the policy drift - improves performance in off-policy settings
   - **Novel local search with replay buffer (LS)** - Uses parallel MALA steps to generate high-quality samples stored in a buffer, then trains the sampler on backward trajectories leading to those samples. This prevents mode collapse and improves sample quality.

**Experimental results on unconditional sampling tasks (25GMM, Funnel, Manywell, LGCP):**
- TB with exploration and local search (LS) substantially improves performance, competing with or surpassing GFlowNet and non-GFlowNet baselines
- Langevin parametrization (LP) consistently improves TB and FL-SubTB, though it is 2-3× slower per iteration
- Local search (LS) effectively prevents mode collapse (Fig. 1)
- Exploration variance should be decayed during training (Fig. 2)

**Conditional sampling (VAE posterior):**
- VarGrad objective with LP and LS achieves competitive performance with simulation-based PIS
- TB-based methods struggle due to difficulty fitting the conditional log-partition function

**Extensions:** The implementation supports learning the backward (noising) process, learning forward diffusion rates, and using varying noise schedules. Learning the forward policy variance significantly improves performance with fewer discretization steps (Fig. 3).

1 Contingency-Aware Spatiotemporal Optimization for Safe Autonomous Vehicle Trajectory Planning Zhihao Lin1, Jianglin Lan1,§, Anh-Tu Nguyen2, Senior Member, IEEE, and David Flynn1 Abstract—Autonomous lane changing requires balancing safety, comfort, and efficiency while managing complex spa-tiotemporal vehicle interactions. Current methods often sepa-rate risk assessment from trajectory planning, leading to ei-ther conservative or unsafe maneuvers. This paper presents a contingency-aware spatiotemporal optimization framework that integrates dynamic risk assessment and trajectory optimization to ensure the autonomous host vehicle (HV) achieve safer, more efficient lane changes. First, the HV uses a dynamic risk field method to assess the collision risk with surrounding vehicles (SVs) in real-time, integrating dynamic obstacle interactions through modified Gaussian distributions. Second, a spatiotemporal safety corridor construction scheme leverages regression-based bound-aries to transform spatiotemporal requirements into manageable optimization constraints. Third, the HV adopts a contingency-aware model predictive control framework that incorporates SVs uncertainty for human-like lane changes. The formulated optimization problem is solved using sequential quadratic pro-gramming with stability and recursive feasibility. Simulations confirm that our approach ensures safety and comfort of the HV across lane changing scenarios, achieving smoother trajectories, improved stability, and enhanced safety margins, with up to 95% reductions in longitudinal and lateral accelerations and a 27% decrease in lane-changing time.
Index Terms—Autonomous vehicle, dynamic risk field, lane changing, model predictive control, trajectory planning.
I. INTRODUCTION A UTONOMOUS vehicles (AVs) have demonstrated sig-nificant potential in enhancing transportation safety and efficiency by reducing human errors and improving decision-making accuracy [1]. Lane changing represents one of the most challenging autonomous driving tasks, due to its requirement for real-time decision making while considering complex interactions with multiple surrounding vehicles (SVs) [2], [3].
During such maneuvers, the autonomous host vehicle (HV) faces numerous challenges (see Fig. 1): following a lead SV too conservatively may result in missed opportunities, while aggressive lane changes could lead to collision with SVs in the target lane [4], [5]. Traditional approaches treating lane changing and car-following as separate processes often leading to in-consistent or suboptimal behaviors [7], [8]. In lane changes, autonomous HVs must balance dynamic interactions and static constraints to choose collision-free paths [9], [10], demanding a unified approach that addresses both immediate safety and long-term trajectory planning [11].
Existing research on autonomous lane changing is broadly categorized into rule-based, learning-based, and optimization-based methods. Rule-based methods [12], [13] use predefined criteria for lane changes, offering efficiency but struggling in complex or unexpected traffic scenarios. Learning-based methods [14]–[17] handle diverse traffic by learning from data but face key challenges: 1) lack of formal safety guarantees, 2) limited interpretability, and 3) unpredictability in unseen scenarios [18], [19]. Optimization-based methods structure planning as constrained problems, but often use simplistic risk models that overlook dynamic traffic interactions.
Recent advancements have explored situation-based plan-ning methods that integrate predictive capabilities with formal guarantees [20]. Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT) and its variants generate space-filling trees for AV navigation [21], [22], aiding in obstacle avoidance. However, they face issues like slow convergence, high computational cost in complex spaces, and jerky, suboptimal trajectories [23]. Voronoi-based methods [24], [25] are efficient and safe in static settings, but struggle with dynamic obstacles and sparse sampling. The Artificial Potential Field (APF) method [26] offers intuitive obstacle avoidance, but often causes unstable trajectories and local minima traps [27]. Though better than traditional meth-ods, these situation-based approaches focus on current states and lack foresight for evolving traffic [28], [29].
2 Predictive optimization methods, like nonlinear model pre-dictive control (NMPC), incorporate future state estimation for trajectory planning [30], [31]. However, NMPC faces chal-lenges: 1) high computational cost, 2) sensitivity to prediction errors, and 3) difficulty modeling interactive behaviors [32].
Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) methods balance explo-ration and exploitation to handle large state spaces [13], [14], but tightly coupling decision-making and planning hinders verification and error recovery. Space-time planning [12] is theoretically elegant but relies on simplified risk models and faces scalability issues in complex traffic.
A key gap in current literature is the separation of risk as-sessment and trajectory planning. Though some integrate risk metrics [33], they rely on simple models that miss complex spatial-temporal interactions in lane changing. Additionally, most treat SVs as reactive, not interactive agents [34], [35].
This leads to systems that are either overly conservative, missing opportunities, or too aggressive, risking safety in dynamic traffic.
To tackle these challenges, we propose an autonomous lane-changing framework integrating dynamic risk assessment, spatiotemporal safety corridors, and contingency-aware trajec-tory optimization. Simulations show our method outperforms existing ones by reducing acceleration variations and main-taining safety across scenarios. The main contributions and innovations of this work are: 1) We develop a dynamic risk field (DRF) method that combines static and dynamic risks using modified Gaus-sian distributions, reshaping risk distributions by motion direction for anticipatory assessment with a smooth, differentiable model capturing complex spatiotemporal interactions.
2) We introduce an innovative spatiotemporal safety corri-dor approach with regression-based boundary estimation that adaptively constructs phase-dependent safety regions, automatically activating relevant constraints based on the vehicle’s position during lane transitions without requir-ing extensive training data or predetermined templates.
3) We propose a contingency-aware NMPC framework that incorporates the prediction uncertainty for SVs. The framework adapts trajectory optimization by selecting the best path based on anticipated responses of the target lane’s rear SV, resulting in safer lane changes even under significant behavioral uncertainty.
The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section II presents the problem formulation and system architecture.
Section III details the dynamic risk awareness. Section IV de-scribes spatiotemporal safety corridor construction. Section V describes the trajectory optimization framework. Section VI presents simulation results and comparative analysis, and Section VII concludes the paper.

3) DRF Construction: The traditional APF typically model obstacles as static repulsive forces and they often struggle with dynamic environments due to their limited ability to model temporal interactions. Conversely, learning-based approaches can capture complex patterns but frequently lack interpretabil-ity and theoretical guarantees [36]. Our DRF method bridges this gap by extending Gaussian-based risk representations with explicit modeling of dynamic interactions through a velocity-dependent component.
Unlike existing methods that simply scale static risk fields based on relative velocity magnitude [37], our approach fundamentally reshapes the risk distribution based on both the magnitude and direction of relative motion. Table I presents the parameter values used in our DRF formulation, which were determined through a combination of theoretical analysis and extensive experimental validation to ensure effective risk assessment across diverse traffic scenar-ios. The static risk amplitude As is set higher than the dynamic risk amplitude Ad to prioritize immediate collision risks over potential future conflicts. The shape parameter β = 2 creates a risk field that balances between a steep Gaussian (β = 1) and a broader platykurtic distribution, providing appropriate risk gradients for optimization. The spatial standard deviations σx and σy were selected based on typical highway lane widths (3.5–3.7 m) and vehicle dimensions, while σv scales with relative velocity to accurately represent the increased risk at higher closing speeds. The position influence factor α determines the asymmetry of the DRF, with α = 2 creating a forward-shifted risk profile that anticipates motion. The influence decay distance de was set to ensure sufficient risk perception range while maintaining computational efficiency.
To validate the sensitivity of these parameters, we con-ducted a series of tests by varying each parameter within ±30% of its nominal value. The results indicated that the risk field maintains robustness across reasonable parameter variations, with performance degradation less than 5% in terms of safety margins and comfort metrics. The dynamic risk coefficient kv and shape parameter β were found to be the most sensitive parameters, requiring careful tuning to balance safety conservatism with trajectory optimization efficiency.

V. TRAJECTORY OPTIMIZATION This section formulates the lane changing trajectory plan-ning as a constrained NMPC problem that incorporates pre-diction of the SV2. Unlike traditional approaches that either assume fixed motion patterns or full cooperation for SVs, we recognize that vehicles (whether HDVs or AVs) naturally respond to merging maneuvers while maintaining their own preferences [40]. This observation motivates the proposal of a prediction-aware planning framework that adapts to SV2’s potential responses for safer and more efficient lane changes.
A. Planning Strategy with Contingency Handling To implement this prediction-aware planning strategy, we first define the key components of our NMPC formulation.
The problem is structured around the combined state space of both the HV and the target lane rear vehicle (SV2), allowing us to explicitly consider their coupled dynamics and interactions.
Below, we detail the state and control variables, along with the discretized system dynamics that form the foundation of our optimization framework. We adapt standard NMPC to the lane changing scenario where the stage cost incorporates multiple objectives including comfort, safety, and efficiency, while the constraints ensure collision avoidance through spatiotemporal safety corridors in (16). args.summary:
This paper presents a contingency-aware spatiotemporal optimization framework for autonomous vehicle lane changing that integrates dynamic risk assessment and trajectory optimization. The framework consists of three key components: (1) a Dynamic Risk Field (DRF) method that combines static and velocity-dependent risks using modified Gaussian distributions to model complex spatiotemporal interactions with surrounding vehicles; (2) a spatiotemporal safety corridor construction scheme that uses regression-based boundaries to transform safety requirements into optimization constraints; and (3) a contingency-aware Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC) framework that incorporates prediction uncertainty of surrounding vehicles, particularly the target lane rear vehicle (SV2), by considering three scenarios (yield, constant, accelerate) with dynamically evaluated probabilities.

The optimization problem is solved using Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) with stability and recursive feasibility guarantees. Simulations conducted in MATLAB 2023b compared the proposed approach against SQP, Active Set, and Genetic Algorithm baselines in multiple lane-changing scenarios. Results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves up to 95% reductions in longitudinal and lateral accelerations, a 27% decrease in lane-changing time (4.84s vs 6.63s for baselines), smoother trajectories, improved stability, and enhanced safety margins. The framework adapts to different SV2 acceleration scenarios, maintaining safety while balancing efficiency and comfort. The convergence analysis shows consistent cost reduction, monotonic decrease in primal/dual infeasibility, and linear decay of the Lyapunov function.

") [Versions Notes](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9/notes) ## Highlights **What are the main findings?** * The paper presents a unified overview of RL-based lane-changing systems by linking maneuver taxonomy, algorithm families, simulators, and evaluation metrics into one structured framework. * A comparative analysis shows that no single RL paradigm suits all driving scenarios, revealing distinct trade-offs among value-based, policy-based, actor–critic, model-based, and hybrid methods. **What are the implications of the main findings?** * The findings highlight the need for integrated designs that combine RL with safety layers (e.g., MPC/CBFs), cooperative multi-agent decision-making, and explainable mechanisms to ensure trustworthy deployment. * The results motivate the development of standardized evaluation benchmarks and simulation-to-real adaptation strategies to improve robustness and real-world applicability of RL-based lane-changing systems. ## Abstract Autonomous lane-changing is one of the most critical and complex tasks in automated driving. Recent progress in reinforcement learning (RL) has shown strong potential to help autonomous vehicles (AVs) make safe and flexible lane-change decisions in real time under uncertain traffic conditions. In the current studies, there is a lack of a common structure that links RL algorithms, simulation tools, and performance evaluation methods. This paper presents a detailed examination of RL-based lane-changing systems in AVs, tracing their development from early rule-based models to modern learning-based approaches. It introduces a clear classification of lane-changing types—discretionary, mandatory, cooperative, and emergency—and connects each to the most suitable RL methods, including value-based, policy-based, actor–critic, model-based, and hybrid algorithms. Each method is examined for its performance, safety, and computational demands. Furthermore, it reviews major simulation environments, such as SUMO, CARLA, and SMARTS, and summarizes key evaluation measures related to safety, efficiency, comfort, and real-time performance. The comparison shows open research challenges, including model adaptation, safety assurance, and transfer from simulation to real-world driving. Finally, it outlines promising directions for future work, such as cooperative decision-making, safe and explainable RL, and lightweight models for real-time use. This review provides a clear foundation and practical guide for developing reliable and understandable RL-based lane-changing systems for future intelligent transportation. Keywords: [autonomous vehicles](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=autonomous+vehicles); [lane-changing maneuvers](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=lane-changing+maneuvers); [reinforcement learning](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=reinforcement+learning); [decision-making systems](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=decision-making+systems); [RL algorithms](https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=RL+algorithms) ## 1. Introduction AVs have become a defining element of modern Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS), which offer the potential to improve road safety, reduce congestion, and improve transportation efficiency [[1](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B1-smartcities-09-00009)]. By integrating advanced perception, connectivity, and artificial intelligence (AI), AVs are progressing steadily towards higher levels of autonomy. Even with remarkable advances in sensing that make decisions and control, achieving full Level 5 autonomy under the SAE framework remains an unsolved and ongoing research challenge. Current systems show partial-autonomy Tesla vehicles operate at Level 2.5, while Audi has introduced Level 3 features [[2](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B2-smartcities-09-00009)]. At the same time, companies such as Waymo, Cruise, FiveAI, and Oxbotica continue to advance higher-level automation with promising results [[3](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B3-smartcities-09-00009)]. [Figure 1](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#fig_body_display_smartcities-09-00009-f001) illustrates the SAE framework of vehicle autonomy, spanning from basic driver assistance to complete autonomy. ![Image 8: Smartcities 09 00009 g001](https://www.mdpi.com/smartcities/smartcities-09-00009/article_deploy/html/images/smartcities-09-00009-g001-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#fig_body_display_smartcities-09-00009-f001) **Figure 1.** SAE Levels of AV. Among many tasks in automated driving, lane-changing continues to be one of the most complex and safety-critical maneuvers. It required real-time coordination, lateral and longitudinal control, dynamic decision-making, and adaptation to uncertain traffic environments [[4](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B4-smartcities-09-00009)]. According to World Health Organization (WHO) data, about 1.35 million people die in road accidents each year, with human error accounting for nearly 95% of accidents. Improper lane-changing alone contributes to an estimated 240,000–610,000 accidents yearly [[5](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B5-smartcities-09-00009),[6](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B6-smartcities-09-00009),[7](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B7-smartcities-09-00009)], emphasizing the urgent need for intelligent and reliable automated solutions. In the past two decades, lane-changing research has moved from rule-based and model-driven approaches to learning-based decision-making methods [[8](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B8-smartcities-09-00009)]. As a result, lane-changing is widely studied as a separate and important decision-making problem, especially in highway and merging scenarios. Recent developments in Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) and AI have opened new opportunities for autonomous driving to become one of the most effective approaches [[9](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B9-smartcities-09-00009)]. RL enables AVs to optimize decision strategies through continuous interaction with their environment, adapting in real time to the evolving traffic dynamics. RL provides a strong and flexible way to handle uncertainty and the fast-changing nature of lane changes by learning from direct feedback [[10](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B10-smartcities-09-00009)]. In recent research, RL has been applied to lane-changing decisions using different algorithm types and simulation platforms. Most studies focus on improving safety, efficiency, or comfort in simulated environments [[11](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B11-smartcities-09-00009)]. However, these works often use different problem settings, traffic scenarios, and evaluation metrics, which makes comparison difficult. Existing survey papers usually discuss autonomous driving in general, while lane-changing is treated only briefly and without a unified structure. At the macroscopic level, RL-based control helps improve overall traffic safety and efficiency by keeping traffic flow smooth and increasing throughput [[12](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B12-smartcities-09-00009)]. At the microscopic level, it reduces sudden acceleration, shortens travel time, and enhances passenger comfort through smoother, more coordinated motion [[13](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B13-smartcities-09-00009)]. When combined with rich sensor data and vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communication, RL allows vehicles to process large amounts of real-time information, coordinate with others, and perform efficient lane changes in constantly changing traffic conditions [[14](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B14-smartcities-09-00009),[15](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B15-smartcities-09-00009)]. With all these strengths, research on RL-based lane-changing remains uncoordinated. Most existing surveys examine autonomous driving in general terms, offering only limited attention to lane-changing as a distinct decision-making problem. There is still no unified taxonomy of algorithms, comparative analysis of simulation environments, or consistent evaluation framework. This makes progress slow, obscures limitations, and limits the identification of future research directions. The main contributions in this paper are summarized as follows: * A comprehensive review of RL models for autonomous lane-changing, organized around a structured taxonomy of maneuver types. * An identification of the key challenges, including environmental complexity, safety assurance, and ethical considerations, with analyze how these challenges affect the practical suitability of different RL algorithm families. * A comparative analysis of major RL algorithm families, focusing on how their design choices influence safety, efficiency, comfort, robustness, and real-time feasibility in lane-changing. * An overview of simulation platforms and evaluation metrics for RL-based lane-changing and analyze their interdependencies and limitations, with particular attention to simulation-to-reality transfer. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. [Section 2](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#sec2-smartcities-09-00009) reviews the evolution of lane-changing models, the AV architectures. [Section 3](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#sec3-smartcities-09-00009) introduces a taxonomy of lane-changing maneuvers, and [Section 4](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#sec4-smartcities-09-00009) surveys RL algorithms. [Section 5](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#sec5-smartcities-09-00009) discusses major challenges. [Section 6](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#sec6-smartcities-09-00009) summarizes simulation tools, and [Section 7](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#sec7-smartcities-09-00009) metrics of valuation. [Section 8](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#sec8-smartcities-09-00009) provides comparative analyses, followed by a discussion of current limitations and future research directions in [Section 9](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#sec9-smartcities-09-00009) and [Section 10](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#sec10-smartcities-09-00009), respectively. This paper concludes in [Section 11](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#sec11-smartcities-09-00009). ## 2. Background ### 2.1. Evolution of Lane-Changing Models Lane-changing is the main area for research into traffic behavior, evolving from rule-based formulations to data-driven and learning-based paradigms. Gipps [[16](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B16-smartcities-09-00009)] introduced an early model that applied fixed rules to govern speed control and gap selection, offering a structured but simplified view of driver behavior. These models provided a useful understanding of behavior under controlled traffic conditions; however, they lacked the flexibility to capture the random and adaptive nature of human driving [[17](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B17-smartcities-09-00009)]. These deterministic formulations assume rational and homogeneous driver behavior, ignore long-term interaction effects, and cannot adapt their decision logic when traffic conditions deviate from predefined assumptions. As a result, rule-based models struggle in heterogeneous, dense, or adversarial traffic environments where driver intentions evolve dynamically. Researchers introduce probabilistic and incentive-based models to enhance behavioral accuracy. A milestone was the Minimizing Overall Braking Induced by Lane Changes (MOBIL) model by Kesting et al. [[18](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B18-smartcities-09-00009)]. When coupled with the Intelligent Driver Model (IDM) [[19](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B19-smartcities-09-00009)], MOBIL enabled microscopic simulation of interactions by using parameters such as acceleration, politeness, and lane bias. These models offered better behavioral fidelity, but they remained constrained by handcrafted decision rules and limited adaptability to unexpected or dynamic conditions. Although MOBIL improved realism through explicit incentive structures, its decision logic remains static and locally optimized. It depends on manually tuned parameters that do not generalize well across different traffic scenarios. In addition, the model focuses on short-term objectives, such as minimizing immediate braking, rather than balancing safety and efficiency over longer time horizons. This limits its applicability for autonomous systems that must reason about future consequences and evolving traffic interactions. Moving to data-driven modeling marked a significant shift, as early statistical techniques such as logistic regression and linear discriminant analysis were used to infer lane-changing intentions from observed trajectories [[20](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B20-smartcities-09-00009),[21](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B21-smartcities-09-00009)]. More recently, non-linear machine learning approaches—such as random forests, support vector machines, ensemble methods, and deep neural networks—have been widely investigated [[22](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B22-smartcities-09-00009),[23](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B23-smartcities-09-00009)]. While these approaches enhanced prediction accuracy and adaptability, they depended heavily on large annotated datasets and were not inherently designed to optimize long-term decision outcomes. Most supervised learning approaches treat lane-changing as a classification or regression problem, separating perception from decision-making. This separation limits their ability to actively reason about future consequences, interaction feedback, and sequential risk accumulation. Moreover, their reliance on offline datasets introduces dataset bias and restricts generalization to unseen scenarios, including rare but safety-critical events. This limitation motivated the adoption of RL, which enables an autonomous agent to refine lane-changing policies through iterative interaction with its environment. RL refines strategies through iterative trial-and-error processes guided by reward signals. The capacity of RL for continuous adaptation and optimization under uncertainty makes it a natural progression from static, rule-based frameworks toward intelligent, self-improving decision-making systems [[24](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B24-smartcities-09-00009),[25](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B25-smartcities-09-00009)]. Unlike previous paradigms, RL explicitly formulates lane-changing as a sequential decision-making problem, where actions influence future states and rewards. This represents a fundamental paradigm shift—from reactive or predictive modeling toward goal-driven policy optimization—allowing AVs to balance safety, efficiency, comfort, and interaction over long time horizons. By learning directly from environmental feedback rather than predefined rules or static labels, RL enables scalable, adaptive, and context-aware decision-making that is essential for real-world autonomous driving. ### 2.2. AV System An AV works through a layered structure that combines perception, communication, decision-making, and control to ensure safe and reliable driving. As shown in [Figure 2](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#fig_body_display_smartcities-09-00009-f002), these modules work as connected stages, where the accuracy of the sensors directly affects how well the vehicle makes its driving decisions [[26](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B26-smartcities-09-00009)]. ![Image 9: Smartcities 09 00009 g002](https://www.mdpi.com/smartcities/smartcities-09-00009/article_deploy/html/images/smartcities-09-00009-g002-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#fig_body_display_smartcities-09-00009-f002) **Figure 2.** Architecture of the AV lane-change system. The perception module collects data from sensors such as LiDAR, radar, cameras, GPS, and IMUs to detect and follow nearby vehicles and obstacles. By combining data from different sensors, it constructs a dynamic representation of the environment and predicts nearby agents’ trajectories. These functions are further improved by V2X communication [[27](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B27-smartcities-09-00009)], which lets vehicles share information with the road system and other cars, increasing awareness and the accuracy of decisions. Based on these sensor inputs, the decision-making module determines whether, when, and how to initiate a lane change. It considers local traffic density, route planning objectives, and traffic-rule compliance to select a feasible and safe maneuver [[28](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B28-smartcities-09-00009)]. The design of this module can follow either a decentralized or centralized approach. In a decentralized setup, each vehicle makes its own decisions, which provides flexibility and easy expansion but requires robust coordination to avoid conflicts [[29](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B29-smartcities-09-00009)]. In contrast, centralized systems manage multiple vehicles through a main control unit, enabling overall optimization but increasing communication and computing costs, especially in dense traffic conditions [[30](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B30-smartcities-09-00009)]. The control layer executes the selected maneuver by coordinating lateral control (steering and side movement) with longitudinal control (acceleration and braking). This ensures the vehicle tracks the planned path smoothly and safely while maintaining comfort and adherence to traffic laws [[31](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B31-smartcities-09-00009)]. Together, these layers show that decision-making—positioned between perception and control—is the most critical stage for achieving safe and efficient lane changes. This highlights the increasing importance of adaptive learning methods like RL, which can interpret complex traffic contexts and refine decisions through experience rather than fixed programming. ### 2.3. RL in AV RL formulates driving as a sequential decision problem under uncertainty. RL is different from supervised learning, where the agents learn directly from environmental interaction through reward feedback, making it particularly suitable for dynamic, continuous control tasks such as lane-changing, as shown in [Figure 3](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#fig_body_display_smartcities-09-00009-f003). ![Image 10: Smartcities 09 00009 g003](https://www.mdpi.com/smartcities/smartcities-09-00009/article_deploy/html/images/smartcities-09-00009-g003-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#fig_body_display_smartcities-09-00009-f003) **Figure 3.** RL framework for autonomous lane-changing decision-making. Formally, the RL process is characterized by a Markov Decision Process (MDP) that is characterized by the tuple $\left(S , A , P , R , \gamma\right)$, where $S$ is the set of states, $A$ the set of actions, $P$ the transition probability function, $R$ the reward function, and $\gamma \in \left[0,1\right]$ is the discount factor balancing short- and long-term rewards. The objective is to learn a policy $\pi \textrm{ } * \left(a∣s\right)$ that maximizes the expected cumulative return. $$ J \left(\pi\right) = E_{\pi} \left[\sum_{t = 0}^{\infty} \gamma^{t} R_{t + 1}\right] $$ (1) The value function $V^{\pi} \left(s\right)$ and action-value function $Q^{\pi} \left(s , a\right)$ estimate the expected return when following policy $\pi$. The optimal policy $\pi \textrm{ } *$ is obtained by maximizing $Q^{\pi} \left(s , a\right)$ all actions. Real-world driving often violates the complete observation assumption of MDPs. In practice, autonomous vehicles operate under the mathematical model Partially Observable MDPs (POMDPs) because of sensor noise, occlusions, and the behavioral uncertainty of other drivers. The agent uses this model to keep track maintain a belief distribution $b \left(s\right)$ over possible states and seeks an optimal policy that maximizes expected return over these belief states: $$ \pi^{*} = arg \underset{\pi}{max} \mathbb{E}_{b \left(s\right)} \left[R \left(s , a\right)\right] $$ (2) This formulation captures the stochasticity of real traffic and enables AVs to act reliably despite incomplete information. The adaptive and reliable nature of RL positions it as one of the most promising approaches for decision-making in AV lane-changing. Therefore, applying these learned policies to real-world driving continues to present a major challenge. ## 3. Lane-Changing Maneuvers in AV Lane-changing requires accurate and timely coordination among perception, planning, and control, especially in dynamic and uncertain traffic environments. The success of lane changes is fundamental not only for ensuring passenger safety but also for maintaining smooth traffic flow—particularly on highways [[32](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B32-smartcities-09-00009)], urban road networks [[33](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B33-smartcities-09-00009)], and merging zones [[34](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B34-smartcities-09-00009),[35](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B35-smartcities-09-00009)]. The successful execution of a lane change depends on how well the vehicle systems work together to understand the environment, predict risks, and perform smooth transitions. ### 3.1. Classification of Lane-Changing Maneuvers In autonomous driving, lane-changing maneuvers are commonly classified into four principal categories, each defined by its underlying motivation, intended outcome, and degree of vehicle interaction. Among these, discretionary lane change (DLC) is initiated for comfort or efficiency, such as when a vehicle shifts to a faster lane to improve travel time and driving smoothness [[36](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B36-smartcities-09-00009)]. He et al. [[37](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B37-smartcities-09-00009)] examined the dynamic characteristics of discretionary lane changes and observed that, while DLCs can enhance individual mobility, they may simultaneously disrupt the overall stability of traffic flow. Mandatory lane change (MLC) is the second category that is driven by external constraints, such as approaching highway exits, lane closures, or a mandatory merging zone [[21](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B21-smartcities-09-00009)]. In these situations, the vehicle must complete the lane change within a limited spatial and temporal window. Cao et al. [[38](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B38-smartcities-09-00009)] proposed an RL-based planning framework for highway exiting that explicitly accounts for safety constraints during forced lane changes. The third category is cooperative lane change (CLC), which uses explicit or implicit coordination with other vehicles that is supported by V2V communication or vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) [[30](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B30-smartcities-09-00009),[39](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B39-smartcities-09-00009)]. Zhou et al. [[40](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B40-smartcities-09-00009)] applied multi-agent RL (MARL) to enable cooperative behavior among AVs, making them work together to negotiate gaps, adjust their speeds, and perform smoother merges compared to vehicles that act independently. The final category is emergency lane change (ELC), which is executed under imminent risk, such as sudden obstacles, unexpected braking, or potential collisions [[27](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B27-smartcities-09-00009)]. Dai et al. [[41](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B41-smartcities-09-00009)] examined emergency lane-changing under collision-avoidance constraints, emphasizing the need for rapid, reliable decisions where even small errors may have severe consequences. [Table 1](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#table_body_display_smartcities-09-00009-t001) compares these four types based on their objectives, urgency, decision complexity, interaction requirements, and safety considerations. The comparison shows that no single decision strategy can address all situations. DLC and MLC focus more on efficiency and rule compliance, while CLC and ELC prioritize cooperation and safety. Therefore, variety and adaptable decision-making frameworks—such as RL—are useful, as they can adjust the vehicle’s behavior according to the situation and safety needs. **Table 1.** Comparative characteristics of lane-changing maneuver categories (DLC, MLC, CLC, ELC). ![Image 11](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#table_body_display_smartcities-09-00009-t001) ### 3.2. Challenges in Lane-Changing Maneuvers Each lane change requires a precise balance between safety, efficiency, and following traffic rules. These decisions often need to be made quickly and in changing traffic conditions. The challenges are most noticeable on highways [[32](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B32-smartcities-09-00009)], in heavy traffic [[29](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B29-smartcities-09-00009)], or when dealing with unpredictable human drivers [[42](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B42-smartcities-09-00009)]. A central challenge is perception uncertainty. Autonomous vehicles depend on sensors such as LiDAR, radar, and cameras to understand their surroundings. However, these sensors can be affected by bad weather, low light, or blocked views. When perception is inaccurate, the vehicle may get an incomplete picture of its environment, making it harder to predict how other vehicles will move and increasing the chance of unsafe or inefficient maneuvers [[15](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B15-smartcities-09-00009)]. To handle this issue, a strong sensor-fusion and motion-prediction system is needed to keep performance reliable under all conditions. Another central challenge is balancing safety and efficiency. Cautious driving policies focus on safety by avoiding risky maneuvers and keeping larger gaps between vehicles [[30](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B30-smartcities-09-00009)]. This approach reduces collision probability; it can also delay merging or overtaking, causing inefficient traffic flow and potential frustration for human drivers. On the other hand, aggressive strategies that aim for higher efficiency can produce faster lane transitions but increase collision risk and reduce overall road safety [[43](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B43-smartcities-09-00009)]. Finding the right balance between safety and efficiency remains one of the main challenges in autonomous vehicle decision-making. In addition, AVs face legal and ethical complexities related to lane-changing behavior. Following traffic laws is vital for maintaining safety and building public trust in AVs [[44](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B44-smartcities-09-00009)]. However, law alone cannot resolve ethical dilemmas that arise in critical situations—such as unavoidable collisions—where the decision-making system must weigh the safety of vehicle occupants against that of other road users. These morally sensitive situations underscore the need for transparent, explainable, and consensus-driven frameworks that define how AVs should act when ethical priorities conflict. Overall, these challenges show the limit of rule-based or supervised learning methods. Effective lane-changing requires algorithms that are able to operate under uncertainty, adapt to changing traffic, and balance multiple conflicting objectives. RL offers a compelling solution by enabling AVs to learn adaptive policies through continuous interaction with their environment, leading to safer, more efficient, and context-aware maneuver execution. ## 4. RL Algorithms in Lane-Changing RL methods applied to lane-changing can be grouped into five families: value-based, policy-based, actor–critic, model-based, and hybrid approaches. These families differ in how they represent and learned policies, as well as in how they balance efficiency, stability, and adaptability in safety-critical driving contexts. Value-based and policy-based methods form the foundational learning paradigms, while actor–critic approaches integrate both to improve learning stability in continuous decision spaces. Model-based methods explicitly incorporate system dynamics and constraints, whereas hybrid approaches combine multiple strategies to balance safety, adaptability, and computational efficiency. The following provides a structured comparison of these paradigms and their suitability for different lane-changing scenarios. ### 4.1. Value-Based Methods Value-based methods learn an action-value function that estimates the expected cumulative rewards for each state–action pair. It is suited to discrete action spaces but encounters scalability issues in high-dimensional environments and continuous driving domains. Q-Learning [[45](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B45-smartcities-09-00009)] is the foundational value-based algorithm using the Bellman optimality equation to update the optimal action-value function $Q^{*} \left(s , a\right)$ iteratively: $$ Q^{*} \left(s , a\right) = \mathbb{E} \left[r + \gamma \underset{a^{'}}{max} Q^{*} \left(s^{'} , a^{'}\right)∣s , a\right] $$ (3) Here, $\mathbb{E}$ is the expectation over state transitions. Q-Learning approximates $Q^{*} \left(s , a\right)$ updating value estimates based on observed rewards and predicted future returns. $$ Q \left(s , a\right) \leftarrow Q \left(s , a\right) + \mathsf{\alpha} \left[r + \gamma \underset{a^{'}}{max} Q \left(s^{'} , a^{'}\right) - Q \left(s , a\right)\right] $$ (4) where $\mathsf{\alpha} \in \left(0,1\right]$ is the learning rate, and $r + \gamma \underset{a^{'}}{max} Q \left(s^{'} , a^{'}\right)$ serve as the target value, although conceptually simple and effective for small-scale problems, where classical Q-learning does not scale well to the rich state spaces encountered in realistic lane-changing scenarios. Deep Q-Networks (DQN) [[46](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B46-smartcities-09-00009)] extend Q-learning to high-dimensional state spaces by approximating $Q \left(s , a ; \theta\right)$ with deep neural networks. The training objective minimizes the following loss: $$ L_{i} \left(\theta_{i}\right) = \mathbb{E}_{s , a , r , s^{'}} \left[\left(r + \gamma \underset{a^{'}}{\mathit{max}} Q \left(s^{'} , a^{'} ; \theta_{i}^{-}\right) - Q \left(s , a ; \theta_{i}\right)\right)^{2}\right] $$ (5) where $\theta_{i}$ denotes a target-network parameter that helps reduce divergence due to correlated samples. For lane-changing, DQN variants have shown good performance in structured scenarios where the decision is essentially “when and to which lane to move”, but they inherit several limitations: overestimation bias, sensitivity to hyperparameters, and difficulty handling truly continuous steering and acceleration. Improvements such as Double DQN (DDQN) [[47](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B47-smartcities-09-00009)] reduce overestimation by decoupling action selection from value estimation, making it more accurate value estimates and improving stability. The update becomes: $$ Q \left(s , a ; \theta_{i}\right) \leftarrow r + \gamma Q \left(s^{'} , \mathit{arg} \underset{a^{'}}{\mathit{max}} Q \left(s^{'} , a^{'} ; \theta_{i}\right) ; \theta_{i}^{-}\right) $$ (6) Dueling DQN [[48](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B48-smartcities-09-00009)] further refines representation by decomposing the Q-function into a state-value component $V \left(s\right)$ and an advantage component $A \left(s , a\right)$. $$ Q \left(s , a ; \theta , \alpha , \beta\right) = V \left(s ; \theta , \beta\right) + \left(A \left(s , a ; \theta , \alpha\right) - \frac{1}{\left|A\right|} \underset{a^{'}}{\sum} A \left(s , a^{'} ; \theta , \alpha\right)\right) $$ (7) Here, $V \left(s\right)$ captures how good a state is, irrespective of the action, while $A \left(s , a\right)$ model the relative benefit of choosing a particular action in that state, leading to richer value estimates. Prioritized Experience Replay (PER) [[49](https://www.mdpi.com/2624-6511/9/1/9#B49-smartcities-09-00009)] enhances stability and sample efficiency by replaying transitions with larger temporal-difference (TD) errors more frequently. Transitions are sampled with probability $P \left(e_{i}\right) \propto p_{i}^{\alpha}$, with $\mathsf{\alpha} \in \left[0,1\right]$ controlling how strongly prioritization is applied. To correct for sampling, importance-sampling weights $w_{i}$ are used, where $N$ is the replay buffer size, and $\beta \in \left[0,1\right]$ control bias correction. $$ w_{i} = \left(\frac{1}{N} \cdot \frac{1}{P \left(e_{i}\right)}\right)^{\beta} $$ (8) Overall, value-based methods are suitable for discrete high-level decisions (DLC/MLC timing and lane choice); less appropriate as a stand-alone solution for low-level continuous control. ### 4.2. This is an academic survey article titled "Reinforcement Learning for Lane-Changing Decision Making in Autonomous Vehicles: A Survey" published in the journal *Smart Cities* (2026, Volume 9, Issue 1, Article 9). The authors are Ammar Khaleel (Széchenyi István University, Hungary) and Áron Ballagi, published on 3 January 2026 under an open access Creative Commons license.

**Main Findings:**
- The paper presents a unified overview of RL-based lane-changing systems, linking maneuver taxonomy, algorithm families, simulators, and evaluation metrics into one structured framework.
- A comparative analysis shows that no single RL paradigm suits all driving scenarios, revealing distinct trade-offs among value-based, policy-based, actor-critic, model-based, and hybrid methods.

**Implications:**
- Findings highlight the need for integrated designs combining RL with safety layers (e.g., MPC/CBFs), cooperative multi-agent decision-making, and explainable mechanisms.
- Results motivate the development of standardized evaluation benchmarks and simulation-to-real adaptation strategies.

**Abstract Summary:** The paper examines RL-based lane-changing systems in autonomous vehicles, tracing development from rule-based to learning-based approaches. It classifies lane-changing types (discretionary, mandatory, cooperative, emergency) and connects each to suitable RL methods. It reviews simulation environments (SUMO, CARLA, SMARTS) and evaluation measures related to safety, efficiency, comfort, and real-time performance. The paper identifies open challenges including model adaptation, safety assurance, and simulation-to-real-world transfer.

**Key Background:** The paper discusses the evolution of lane-changing models from rule-based (Gipps model, MOBIL/IDM) to data-driven and RL-based approaches. It notes that approximately 1.35 million people die in road accidents yearly, with human error accounting for ~95% of accidents, and improper lane-changing contributing to 240,000-610,000 accidents annually.

**RL Methods Covered:** The paper categorizes RL algorithms into value-based (Q-Learning, DQN, Double DQN, Dueling DQN with Prioritized Experience Replay), policy-based, actor-critic, model-based, and hybrid approaches. The RL framework is formalized as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), with real-world driving modeled as Partially Observable MDPs (POMDPs) due to sensor noise and behavioral uncertainty.

**Lane-Changing Classification:** Four categories are defined: Discretionary Lane Change (DLC), Mandatory Lane Change (MLC), Cooperative Lane Change (CLC), and Emergency Lane Change (ELC).

1 Safety-aware human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning with shared control for autonomous driving Wenhui Huang, Haochen Liu, Zhiyu Huang and Chen Lv, Senior Member, IEEE Abstract—The learning from intervention (LfI) approach has been proven effective in improving the performance of RL algorithms; nevertheless, existing methodologies in this domain tend to operate under the assumption that human guidance is invariably devoid of risk, thereby possibly leading to oscillations or even divergence in RL training as a result of improper demon-strations. In this paper, we propose a safety-aware human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning (SafeHIL-RL) approach to bridge the abovementioned gap. We first present a safety assessment module based on the artificial potential field (APF) model that incorporates dynamic information of the environment under the Frenet coordinate system, which we call the Frenet-based dynamic potential field (FDPF), for evaluating the real-time safety throughout the intervention process. Subsequently, we propose a curriculum guidance mechanism inspired by the pedagogical principle of whole-to-part patterns in human education. The curriculum guidance facilitates the RL agent’s early acquisition of comprehensive global information through continual guidance while also allowing for fine-tuning local behavior through inter-mittent human guidance through a human-AI shared control strategy. Consequently, our approach enables a safe, robust, and efficient reinforcement learning process independent of the quality of guidance human participants provide. The proposed method is validated in two highway autonomous driving sce-narios under highly dynamic traffic flows 1. The experiments’ results confirm the superiority and generalization capability of our approach when compared to other state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines, as well as the effectiveness of the curriculum guidance.
Index Terms—Autonomous driving, human-in-the-loop rein-forcement learning, safe reinforcement learning, curriculum guid-ance, shared control.
I. INTRODUCTION A UTONOMOUS vehicle (AV) is a complicated and holis-tic intelligent system that consists of various ingredients such as perception, decision-making, and planning [1], [2], [3].
Among these components, intelligent decision-making serves as a ”brain” of the AVs to decide where to go and how to go, playing a significant role in achieving fully autonomous driving techniques [4]. Over the past years, scholars have dedicated their efforts to developing such decision-making strategies through various domain knowledge, and in general, these approaches are categorized into two families: rule-based and learning-based methods [5]. In the early stage, the contributions were intensively located on the former one, W. Huang, Z. Huang, H. Liu and C. Lv are with the School of Mechan-ical and Aerospace Engineering, Nanyang Technological University, Singa-pore, 639798. (E-mail: wenhui001@e.ntu.edu.sg, haochen002@e.ntu.edu.sg, zhiyu001@e.ntu.edu.sg, lyuchen@ntu.edu.sg) Corresponding author: C. Lv. (E-mail: lyuchen@ntu.edu.sg) 1https://github.com/OscarHuangWind/Safe-Human-in-the-Loop-RL which employs finite-state machine (FSM) [6] or online op-timization approaches [7], [8] due to their attractive level of interpretability. However, the rule-based method suffers from a significant computational efficiency limitation since the AVs are required to drive under a complex and highly dynamic environment, and it is costly to pre-design the exhausted definitions, as well as the constraints for the different driving scenarios [9]. Alternatively, the learning-based approach has gained growing attention recently due to its superior capabil-ity of handling high-dimensional information. Reinforcement learning (RL) [10] is one of the most widely utilized learning-based approaches for decision-making and control problems in the autonomous driving field [11], [12], [13]. However, the in-trinsic learning mechanism, namely trial-with-error, leads to a significant safety concern that hinders the practical application of the RL-based methods [14].
To address the safety issue mentioned above, a subfield within the RL community entitled Safe RL is proposed [15], [16]. Among various categorized groups within the Safe RL framework, a promising method is leveraging human intel-ligence in the learning loop of the RL algorithms, namely learning from intervention (LfI) [17]. The objective of the LfI approach is to prevent catastrophic actions from occur-ring and replace them with real-time human intervention, guiding the RL agent toward a safe and efficient exploration strategy. Recently, several related works have been proposed and successfully applied to the autonomous navigation [18] and autonomous driving [19] domain. These approaches do not explicitly perform safety assessment since they assume that human beings have the dominant knowledge of the task, and thus, the human demonstration is consistently safe or at least better than that of the RL agents. In reality, however, there is no theoretical guarantee that each human participant has qualified driving proficiency, and it is equally possible that even the experts could perform degraded or catastrophic operations due to various reasons, e.g., degraded attention and intrinsic uncertainty. Therefore, performing a real-time safety assessment for the human demonstration and not entirely relying on human intervention is crucial to the subsequent learning process, especially for the intermediate stage in which the RL agents have learned and possessed a certain level of intelligence.
In light of this, we propose a novel safety-aware human-in-the-loop RL (SafeHIL-RL) framework to bridge the above-mentioned gap. Specifically, we construct a safety module by employing artificial potential field (APF) theory and dynamic information of the environment under the Frenet coordina-tion system, namely the Frenet-based dynamic potential field 2 (FDPF), to perform real-time safety assessment for the human demonstration whenever the intervention occurs. Subsequently, we design a dynamic control authority allocation mechanism to realize the shared autonomy between human participants and RL agents based on the potential hazard level provided by the safety module. Furthermore, we present a curriculum guidance mechanism, which is inspired by the pedagogi-cal principle of whole-to-part patterns in human education, within the proposed framework to facilitate the RL agent’s early acquisition of comprehensive global information through continual guidance while also allowing for fine-tuning lo-cal behavior through intermittent human guidance through a human-AI shared autonomy technique. It is important to highlight that our work does not focus on providing absolute safety assurance for the entire training process since the failure experiences are valuable for RL learning as well.
Instead, SafeHIL-RL aims to present a novel safety-aware LfI approach to prevent policy oscillations or even divergence phenomena caused by inappropriate human demonstrations during the intervention, thereby enhancing learning efficiency and robustness. The proposed method is thoroughly evaluated in the highway autonomous driving scenario with stochastic traffic flow. The experiment and ablation study results confirm the advance of the proposed approach compared to other state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in data efficiency and driving performance. The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows: 1) A novel safety-aware human-in-the-loop RL method within the Safe RL framework is realized by performing the safety assessment over real-time human intervention to enhance the sampling efficiency and quality.
2) A safety module that integrates the APF model and dynamic information of the environment within the Frenet coordination system (FDPF) is presented to eval-uate the real-time risk during the human intervention period. Moreover, a dynamic control authority allocation mechanism is designed to achieve the human-AI shared autonomy approach in the training loop of the RL algorithms.
3) We propose a novel intervention mechanism called curriculum guidance, which draws inspiration from the pedagogical principle of whole-to-part patterns observed in human education. This mechanism aims to encourage the early acquisition of comprehensive global informa-tion by RL agents, followed by the fine-tuning of local behavior in subsequent stages, ultimately guiding the RL learning process towards smoothness and robustness.
4) We instantiated a concrete human-in-the-loop RL algo-rithm for the proposed approach and thoroughly eval-uated it in the highway autonomous driving scenario under stochastic traffic flow, providing an efficient and reliable end-to-end autonomous driving solution.
II. RELATED WORKS In this section, we present a review of the RL-based autonomous driving policy and LfI approach.
A. Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Driving Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown great potential in handling decision-making and control problems in compli-cated environments due to its superior representation capabil-ity. In general, RL algorithms can be categorized into three main groups, the value-based approaches such as deep Q-network (DQN) [20] and its variants [21], [22], [23], [24], policy-based methods like trust region policy optimization (TRPO) [25] and proximal policy optimization (PPO) [26], and actor-critic-based framework such as deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG) [27], twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (TD3) [28], and soft actor-critic (SAC) [29].
Recently, these algorithms have been intensively employed in the autonomous driving field. For instance, [30] successfully realizes the end-to-end decision-making for autonomous ve-hicles in the simulation through the DQN algorithm with the gray-scaled image only. In [31], [32], the DDPG algorithm is utilized to learn autonomous driving strategy by considering traffic rules. Similarly, [33] advances the same algorithm to real-world driving under driver supervision. Subsequently, [34] employs the SAC algorithm to realize the high-speed autonomous drifting function, while [35] addresses the end-to-end control tasks through the SAC algorithm in an urban environment. In [36], a sim-to-real application of autonomous navigation is presented by means of the same algorithm, with the augmented scene encoder called Goal-enabled Transformer (GoT). Moreover, the TD3 algorithm is employed to handle the unprotected left-turn and congestion scenarios for autonomous vehicles in [37].
B. Learning from Intervention Despite the various successful applications, the RL algo-rithms notoriously suffer from poor data efficiency stemming from their intrinsic learning mechanism: trial-with-error. A promising solution for addressing the abovementioned issue is leveraging human intelligence in the training loop of the RL agents. In light of this, [38] proposes a learning from intervention (LfI) approach titled human intervention RL (HIRL) to lead the intelligent agent with a safe exploration strategy by means of avoiding catastrophic actions under human supervision. In the subsequent years, scholars have dedicated themselves to enhancing the LfI approach from various domains. For example, [39] proposes a novel approach entitled expert intervention learning (EIL) to introduce human guidance into the value function as a constraint to achieve a safe autonomous navigation strategy. Instead of augmenting the loss function of the value network, [18] presents an intervention-aided RL (IARL) method that adds an imitation term in the actor network of the PPO algorithm and evaluates the obstacle-avoiding performance in a real UAV platform.
Similarly, in [40], a method called human-guidance-based deep RL (Hug-DRL) is developed to address the end-to-end autonomous driving control tasks. Alternatively, [41] learns the probability of disengagement from the human intervention rather than the deterministic actions, realizing a safe naviga-tion strategy in a sidewalk environment. C. Safety Assessment and Control Authority Allocation Though human participants can react to a complex envi-ronment rapidly, consistent monitoring would fatigue human beings and subsequently affect the guidance quality. In light of this, we propose a novel artificial potential field (APF)-based safety module and design a control authority allocation mechanism to adaptively transfer the control authority based on real-time safety assessment instead of letting the human participant completely dominate the vehicle control whenever the intervention occurs.

While a SOTA trajectory prediction approach may be preferred, it falls beyond the scope of our work. D. Curriculum Guidance In this study, we propose a novel intervention mechanism called curriculum guidance, shown in Fig. 3, to achieve a smooth and robust human-in-the-loop learning process. Specif-ically, during the training phase, human participants have the power to control the vehicle with a Logitech G29 driving set manually. This process begins with continuous guidance for the initial M episodes and transitions to intermittent guidance for the subsequent periods, continuing through to the Kth episode. In the phase of continuous guidance (spanning from 0 to M episodes), participants have the power to take over vehicle control for the duration of an entire episode once intervention occurs. This strategy is designed to encourage the SafeHIL-RL system to gather comprehensive information early on, facilitating its ability to complete the driving task successfully.
Conversely, during the intermittent guidance phase (from M to K episodes), human participants can only offer guidance for critical moments within an episode. This approach helps refine specific behaviors, e.g., decelerating and executing smooth lane changes, adjusting them based on the policy learned thus far. In the self-learning phase (after K episodes), the human participants are asked to completely hand off the vehicle control and motivate the RL agent to enhance the driving policy through self-exploration continuously. It is important to emphasize that insufficient intervention is unlikely to lead to favorable outcomes in the learning process, while excessive intervention can lead to overfitting to the human demonstra-tion. With these considerations in mind, we restrict human intervention to a maximum of three instances within every ten episodes and confine the involvement of human participants 6 to the first 400 episodes (K=400), which accounts for half of the entire training duration. Furthermore, the transition from continuous to intermittent guidance is empirically set at the 200th episode (M=200), where it is observed that the RL agent achieves a level of competency sufficient to complete the whole trajectory, though its performance may not be optimal.
It is important to distinguish curriculum guidance from cur-riculum learning. Curriculum learning is a training approach that introduces a sequence of progressively challenging tasks to facilitate policy learning and tackle the ultimate complex problems effectively [48]. The core idea of curriculum learning revolves around the arrangement of tasks in a manner that allows the policy to learn varying levels of complexity from the algorithm’s perspective. In contrast, the proposed curriculum guidance does not revolve around task or environment com-plexity since the characteristics of the interactive road users are entirely stochastic (traffic flow, speed, and cooperation willingness) throughout the whole learning process. Instead, curriculum guidance centers on researching and enhancing the LfI approaches from the perspective of human experts within the safe RL framework.
By clarifying the distinction between curriculum guidance and curriculum learning, we can better comprehend the spe-cific focus and objectives of each approach in enhancing the reinforcement learning process. While curriculum learning em-phasizes the sequencing of tasks to aid policy learning, which is from the algorithm point of view, curriculum guidance delves into researching how humans can guide the learning process effectively, focusing on the learning patterns from the human perspective. We provide the formal definition of the curriculum guidance in the following.
Definition 1. (Curriculum Guidance) Suppose the RL agent learns optimal policy via E interaction episodes with an environment, and let ℐbe a set of the guidance from the human intervention. Then, the curriculum guidance consists of a sequence of the state-action pairs over two types of interventions, that is, continual guidance ℐ 𝑐= {< 𝑠𝑡, 𝑎H 𝑡 > , · · · , < 𝑠𝑇, 𝑎H 𝑇>} within M episodes and intermittent guid-ance ℐ 𝑖= {< 𝑠𝑡, 𝑎H 𝑡>, · · · , < 𝑠𝜏, 𝑎H 𝜏>} within K episodes, where T and 𝜏denote trajectory and intervention terminal time step, M and K subject to 0 < 𝑀< 𝐾< 𝐸.
Intuitively, such a guidance mechanism is in line with hu-man pedagogy. According to the modes of learning mentioned in [49], the authors mention that the whole-to-part pattern offers an exciting result, encouraging students to prioritize the construction of meaning rather than simply decoding text. For instance, when students acquire new knowledge in school, teachers often acquaint the child with the whole framework first, and then the different portions of it may be analyzed and studied intensively. Therefore, following the above-mentioned principle, the curriculum guidance aims to motivate the SafeHIL-RL to acquire global information over a complete trajectory at the early stage through continual guidance and fine-tuning the local behavior via intermittent human guidance in the subsequent learning process, ultimately guiding toward the smooth and robust RL learning process.

IV. EXPERIMENTS A. Autonomous Driving Scenarios We evaluate the performance of the proposed approach in solving highway autonomous driving issues under dense traffic flows. In this study, two highway scenarios are designed, as shown in Fig. 4. Figure 4(a) demonstrates the first-person and top-down bird’s eye view of the road users and environment where the SafeHIL-RL agent trains its policy. In Fig. 4(b), an additional unobserved highway environment that consists of straight and curve roads is introduced to validate the generalization capability of the post-trained driving policy. In our case, evaluating the performance under curve structure is significant since we would like to confirm that the policy trained by our approach is not over-fitted to the human demonstration under the straight road but learns the causal inference from states to actions.

To replicate authentic highway scenarios, we utilize do-main randomization to introduce randomness in road users’ initial positions, speed distribution, and driving behaviors using Gaussian modeling. Furthermore, these road users have the ability to actively change lanes with varying degrees of willingness to cooperate. By combining all these elements, we regularly generate high-density traffic flows to ensure nearby vehicles are always available for interaction.
B. MDP Formulation In this section, we present the MDP formulation of our approach.
State Space. The 100 × 100 bird-eye view (BEV) top-down images are taken as the image state for the RL agent. The three most recent frames are stacked to enable the temporal perception, and thereby, the dimension of the image state is 100 × 100 × 3. Moreover, we employ the previous actions as the conditional state, encoding it to the latent features and feed to the subsequent networks.
Action Space. The final output of the RL model consists of three elements: pedal, braking, and steering. The pedal and braking values are restricted within the range of 0 to 1, while steering ranges from -1 to 1, representing the left and right directions, respectively.
Reward Function. Our reward function comprises both heuristic and sparse rewards, denoted as: 𝑟(𝑠𝑡, 𝑎𝑡) = 𝑟ℎ+ 𝑟𝑠 (13) The heuristic term in Eq. 13, as a continuous and dense reward, should consider driving efficiency and performance.
Therefore, we shape the heuristic reward as follows: 𝑟ℎ= 𝑟𝑠𝑝𝑒𝑒𝑑+ 𝑟𝑠ℎ𝑜𝑢𝑙𝑑𝑒𝑟+ 𝑟𝑙𝑎𝑛𝑒 (14) where 𝑟𝑠𝑝𝑒𝑒𝑑= 𝜔𝑠𝑝𝑒𝑒𝑑· 𝑣𝑠𝑝𝑒𝑒𝑑encourages the ego vehicle to move forward and 𝑟𝑠ℎ𝑜𝑢𝑙𝑑𝑒𝑟is a small punishment whenever the ego vehicle drive on the shoulder. Moreover, 𝑟𝑙𝑎𝑛𝑒is a cost function that motivates the ego vehicle to keep the lane center an drive along the road direction, calculated as: 𝑟𝑙𝑎𝑛𝑒= −𝜔𝑜𝑓𝑓𝑠𝑒𝑡· (Δ𝑙)2 −𝜔ℎ𝑒𝑎𝑑𝑖𝑛𝑔· (Δ𝜑)2 (15) TABLE I: Parameter Settings for SafeHIL-RL.

The sparse reward is mainly related to the driving task and safety, shaped as follows: 𝑟𝑠= 𝑟𝑔𝑜𝑎𝑙+ 𝑟𝑐𝑜𝑙𝑙𝑖𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛+ 𝑟𝑜𝑓𝑓𝑟𝑜𝑎𝑑 (16) where 𝑟𝑔𝑜𝑎𝑙, 𝑟𝑐𝑜𝑙𝑙𝑖𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛, and 𝑟𝑜𝑓𝑓𝑟𝑜𝑎𝑑are reward for arriving goal position, punishment for collision and drive off the road, denoted as: 𝑟𝑔𝑜𝑎𝑙= ( 3.0, 𝑖𝑓 𝑔𝑜𝑎𝑙𝑟𝑒𝑎𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑑 0, 𝑜𝑡ℎ𝑒𝑟𝑤𝑖𝑠𝑒 𝑟𝑐𝑜𝑙𝑙𝑖𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛= ( −7.0, 𝑖𝑓 𝑐𝑟𝑎𝑠ℎ𝑒𝑑 0, 𝑜𝑡ℎ𝑒𝑟𝑤𝑖𝑠𝑒 𝑟𝑜𝑓𝑓𝑟𝑜𝑎𝑑= ( −7.0, 𝑖𝑓 𝑜𝑓𝑓𝑟𝑜𝑎𝑑 0, 𝑜𝑡ℎ𝑒𝑟𝑤𝑖𝑠𝑒 (17) C. Baseline Algorithms In this paper, we employ several SOTA LfI and RL algo-rithms to thoroughly validate the proposed approach. These baselines are: 1) HIRL: Human intervention reinforcement learning (HIRL) [17] is the first work attempt to formalize online human intervention into the RL framework. The action from the RL agent would be replaced by the one from human policy when human intervention is triggered, avoiding the catastrophic actions that occur during the training.
2) PHIL-RL: The SOTA LfI method known as Prioritized human-in-the-hoop RL (PHIL-RL) [37] aims to address the end-to-end autonomous driving task by incorporating human intelligence into the training process. In con-trast to our proposed approach, the PHIL-RL algorithm employs an takeover strategy when intervention occurs, granting complete control authority to the human. The PHIL-RL utilizes the prioritized replay technique to augment performance, which is not the primary focus of this paper; therefore, we omit the prioritization and concentrate our attention solely on the learning mecha-nism associated with human intervention.

The cornflower-blue dotted line and solid lines represent the aver-age rewards of our approach and baselines per episode, while the shaded areas depict the variances over five runs.
3) SAC: Soft actor-critic (SAC) is a SOTA off-policy RL algorithm that obtains the optimal policy by balancing the overall future payoff and Shannon entropy. In our experiment, we employ the optimal dual version that automatically adjusts the entropy of the behavior policy proposed in [50].
D. Configurations All algorithms are trained on a computer equipped with an Intel Core i7-10700 CPU, 64 GB of RAM, and an NVIDIA GTX 1660 SUPER graphics card. The training process en-compasses 800 episodes, with each episode comprising a maximum of 300 steps. An episode concludes when the target position is reached, a collision transpires, or the ego vehicle exhausts its allotted number of steps. A detailed parameter settings are reported in Table I.
V. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION This section intensively evaluates and presents the training and testing performance of the proposed approach against the SOTA baselines mentioned above, followed by a detailed analysis of the effectiveness of the FDPF and curriculum guidance through an ablation study.
A. Training Performance Figure 5 illustrates the learning curves of SafeHIL-RL and other baselines. We run each algorithm with five different random seeds to measure statistics and evaluate the perfor-mance. The average rewards per episode are represented by the cornflower-blue dotted line for SafeHIL-RL and solid lines with various colors for the baselines. In addition, the shaded areas indicate the variances over the five runs, representing the robustness of each approach. The provided figure reveals that our approach exhibits the fastest convergence rate and achieves the highest level of rewards when compared to other TABLE II: Efficiency Improvement (%) of SafeHIL-RL com-pared with Baselines.
