The pure RL algorithm, the SAC, exhibits the slowest learning process, indicating its limited capability in effectively addressing the complex task of end-to-end au-tonomous driving control in such a challenging environment.
Furthermore, HIRL demonstrates improvement compared to the SAC algorithm in terms of convergence speed, thanks to the integration of human guidance. Conversely, although the reward curve of the PHIL-RL initially displays rapid growth during the early stages where human intervention is allowed, the subsequent learning process without human guidance ex-periences a significant degradation in performance, which is deemed unacceptable within the LfI framework. One potential explanation is that the PHIL-RL approach operates under the assumption that human guidance is consistently reliable during the intervention, leading to an adversarial impact on the actor network when inadequate demonstrations or incorrect guidance is provided. In contrast, our approach effectively addresses this issue by evaluating real-time safety measures, enabling the filtration of improper guidance. As a result, our method ensures a resilient learning process regardless of the guidance quality.
In addition to evaluating the robustness of our training method, we aim to quantitatively assess the superior data efficiency of our approach by calculating the magnitude of average efficiency improvement of SafeHIL-RL compared to baseline methods. This average efficiency improvement metric is computed using the following formula: 𝐸𝑝𝑜𝑐(𝐵𝑎𝑠𝑒|𝑅∗(𝐵𝑎𝑠𝑒)) −𝐸𝑝𝑜𝑐(SafeHIL|𝑅∗(𝐵𝑎𝑠𝑒)) 𝐸𝑝𝑜𝑐(𝐵𝑎𝑠𝑒|𝑅∗(𝐵𝑎𝑠𝑒)) (18) where 𝐸𝑝𝑜𝑐(𝐵𝑎𝑠𝑒|𝑅∗(𝐵𝑎𝑠𝑒) represents the number of the episode the baseline needs to achieve its best reward and 𝐸𝑝𝑜𝑐(SafeHIL|𝑅∗(𝐵𝑎𝑠𝑒)) denotes the number of the episode our approach requires to reach the baseline’s best reward.
The comparison between our method and the baseline ap-proaches is detailed in Table II. It is evident that SafeHIL-RL significantly enhances data efficiency over other LfI and DRL baselines. For example, our method surpasses the PHIL-RL strategy by as much as 71.52% and requires 80.76% less data than the SAC algorithm on average, exhibiting the most superior data efficiency among all approaches.
B. Testing Performance Besides the learning curves, post-trained performance is also a significant metric to evaluate the superiority of the different approaches. To this end, we test the success rate for all the trained policies under scenario I (Fig. 4(a)) with ten additional unobserved seeds and run for twenty episodes for each. The boxplot clearly depicts that the overall performance of our approach completely dominates that of other SOTA baselines in terms of average success rate and corresponding variance, demonstrating superiority and robustness in address-ing end-to-end autonomous driving tasks. Furthermore, we presented the statistical analysis (refer to Table III) of the performance of different algorithms across multiple trials. This analysis allows us to quantitatively evaluate the upper and lower limits of driving performance. Notably, the SafeHIL-RL agent drives the longest distance given the fixed time steps in any case, and most importantly, the performance deviation between the upper and lower bounds is obviously less than that of other baselines. Although the SAC agent exhibited a higher average driving speed compared to the other agents, this was achieved at the expense of a lower success rate, which is entirely undesirable from the safe autonomous driving perspective. As for the keeping lane performance along the lane center, the HIRL agent demonstrated a slightly lower average lateral offset compared to our approach. This can be attributed to the conservative nature of the policy trained by the HIRL method. The HIRL policy tends to slow down and maintain lane position whenever encountering slow-moving leading vehicles. On the contrary, the policy trained by our approach prefers to perform lane-changing behavior to actively get rid of the surrounding vehicles unless the dynamically congested traffic (where all lanes are occupied by slow-moving vehicles) necessitates slowing down. This is also a key reason why the average driving distance of the SafeHIL-RL agent is significantly longer than that of HIRL. These results collectively demonstrate that our proposed approach leads the reinforcement learning (RL) agent to converge towards a more desirable, robust, and safer driving policy compared to SOTA methods.
To confirm the generalization ability and verify whether our approach is overfitted to the human demonstration, we further evaluate the performance of the proposed approach in the unobserved environment, which consists of the 200m straight road and 120m curve, shown in Fig. 4(b). If the performance presented in the Table. III is due to the overfitting of the human guidance, the new road structure, which requires a consistent steering operation unlike the straight road, would significantly challenge the performance of the SafeHIL-RL. In light of this, we tested the performance of the SafeHIL-RL with extra episodes and recorded the ego vehicle’s trajectory information under the Frenet coordinate system. Figure 7 illustrates one example of the recorded data over an entire trajectory. The cornflower blue demonstrates the trajectory of the ego vehicle, while the solid and dashed line in black color represents the lane boundary and center line, respectively. From the figure, we can see that the trained policy under the proposed approach successfully completes the episode without any collision by performing lane-keep and lane-change operations.
Especially we highlight three moments along the trajectory for better demonstration. Figure 7(b) illustrates a dense traffic flow scenario where one of the surrounding vehicles cuts into the ego lane (the lane where the ego vehicle locates).
Motivated by the speed reward and human guidance, the ego vehicle executes the safe lane-change decision, rather than the slow-down operation, to actively get rid of the potential traffic congestion case that may significantly impact driving efficiency. A similar condition on the junction that connects the straight and curve is shown in Fig. 7(c) but with sparser surrounding traffic. In Fig. 7(d), the ego vehicle demonstrates the lane-keep performance on the curve. C. Frenet-based Dynamic Potential Field Visualization In this section, we would like to visualize and highlight the dynamic effect of the proposed FDPF model. One of the key benefits of establishing the safety assessment model based on the Frenet coordination system is that it is straightforward to measure and visualize the potential risk along a curve in the space, no matter the curvature of the road, since the Frenet coordination system uses the arc length of the curve as the reference axis. Moreover, we incorporate the dynamic information of the environment into the safety field modeling, as shown in Eq. 10, to extend or shrink the safety boundary depending on the situation.
We now provide an example to visualize the dynamic effect of the FDPF in Fig. 8. Figure 8(a) illustrates three moments of the highway driving scene captured from one trajectory. From the illustration, we can observe that the ego vehicle encounters a dynamic congested scenario. In this scene, a slow-moving leading vehicle with a speed of only 6.42 m/s is positioned ahead of the ego lane. Additionally, the other two lanes are occupied by vehicles traveling at similar speeds.
The constructed safety field at the first moment is visualized in Fig. 8(b). In this representation, the star denotes the position of the ego vehicle, and the transition from blue to red indicates an increasing potential hazard. In this case, it is evident that the ego vehicle is positioned near the safety boundary with a current driving velocity of 13.59 m/s, which is more than twice the speed of the leading vehicle. However, as the ego vehicle reduces its velocity, the safety boundary of the surrounding road users begins to shrink (Fig. 8(c)). At the third moment (Fig. 8(d)), the situation is deemed significantly safer compared to the first moment. Therefore, despite the relative distance being similar, any acceleration actions at the first moment would be considered potentially dangerous, whereas it is undoubtedly allowed for the third moment, highlighting the reasonable logic and flexibility in the proposed FDPF model.
D. Effect of Curriculum Guidance Despite the fact that we have confirmed the superiority of curriculum guidance against pure continual guidance by comparing the performance with HIRL and PHIL-RL, there could still be uncertainty regarding whether the SafeHIL-RL’s outstanding performance is a result of intermittent guidance rather than curriculum guidance. Therefore, we conduct an additional ablation study regarding the curriculum versus in-termittent guidance. More specifically, we keep all the settings, including the hyperparameter, network structures, intervention times, and safety assessment, but we omit the continual guid-ance mode during training. Thus, human participants are only allowed to intervene intermittently during necessary periods instead of throughout the entire trajectory.
Figure 9 shows the training effort over three seeds. It is clear that the performance of the curriculum guidance completely dominates that of the intermittent guidance, especially at early stage, demonstrating the superiority of the proposed human 11 V𝐴𝑔𝑒𝑛𝑡1= 6.42𝑚/𝑠 V𝐴𝑔𝑒𝑛𝑡2= 6.03𝑚/𝑠 V𝐴𝑔𝑒𝑛𝑡3= 8.0𝑚/𝑠 1 2 3 V = 13.59m/s 1 2 3 V = 10.62m/s 1 2 3 V = 8.14m/s (a) Three moments captured from a trajectory.

guidance mechanism. This phenomenon is not surprising be-cause pure continual guidance can lead to overfitting in the long run, while pure intermittent guidance may lack global information, resulting in a biased future payoff estimation.
In contrast, incorporating curriculum guidance allows for the extraction of benefits from both approaches, effectively addressing the abovementioned issues and leading to a more robust and efficient learning process.
VI. CONCLUSION In this paper, a safety-aware human-in-the-loop reinforce-ment learning (SafeHIL-RL) approach and the concept of cur-riculum guidance are proposed within the safe RL framework.
In order to accomplish this, we present a safety assessment module based on the artificial potential field (APF) model that incorporates dynamic information of the environment under the Frenet coordinate system, which we call the Frenet-based dynamic potential field (FDPF), for evaluating the real-time safety throughout the human-guided learning process. We then introduce a curriculum guidance mechanism inspired by the whole-to-part pattern in pedagogy. This mechanism allows the RL agent to acquire global information early on through continuous guidance and fine-tune local behavior through intermittent human guidance with human-AI shared autonomy.
As a result, the proposed approach enables a safe, robust, and efficient reinforcement learning process, regardless of the qual-ity of guidance provided by human participants. The proposed method is validated in two complex highway autonomous driving scenarios, and the experiment results confirm the superiority and generality, as well as the effectiveness of the curriculum guidance, compared with other SOTA baselines.

args.summary:
This paper presents a safety-aware human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning (SafeHIL-RL) approach for autonomous driving. The key contributions are:

1) **Frenet-based Dynamic Potential Field (FDPF)**: A safety assessment module that integrates artificial potential field (APF) theory with dynamic environmental information under the Frenet coordinate system to evaluate real-time safety during human intervention.

2) **Curriculum Guidance Mechanism**: Inspired by the whole-to-part pedagogical principle, this mechanism has three phases:
   - **Continual guidance** (episodes 0-200): Human participants control the vehicle for entire episodes once intervention occurs, helping the RL agent acquire global information.
   - **Intermittent guidance** (episodes 200-400): Humans provide guidance only for critical moments within episodes, fine-tuning local behavior.
   - **Self-learning** (after 400 episodes): Humans hand off control completely, allowing the agent to improve through self-exploration.

3) **Dynamic Control Authority Allocation**: Based on FDPF safety assessment, control authority is adaptively shared between human and RL agent rather than giving complete control to humans.

The method is validated in two highway scenarios under dense traffic flows using the SMARTS platform. Results show SafeHIL-RL achieves:
- 71.52% efficiency improvement over PHIL-RL
- 28.38% improvement over HIRL
- 80.76% improvement over SAC
- 100% success rate in testing (vs. 70% for PHIL-RL, 90% for HIRL, 75% for SAC)
- Superior generalization to unseen curved road structures

The approach addresses the key limitation of existing LfI methods: the assumption that human guidance is always safe. By performing real-time safety assessment, the method prevents policy oscillations or divergence caused by improper human demonstrations.

## Highlights

*   •Comprehensive evaluation of the safe reinforcement learning (SRL) techniques for the autonomous driving. 
*   •It is essential that safety must be prioritized in the decision-making processes in dynamic road scenarios. 
*   •Detailed discussion on the potential of SRL in autonomous driving and how they can address the challenges posed in traditional RL. 
*   •Highlights the promising impact of SRL for further enhancing the road safety. 

## Abstract

To operate safely in a dynamic environment, autonomous vehicles must possess the same level of predictive driving abilities as human drivers and must be capable of anticipating the future actions of other dynamic objects in the environment, especially those of neighboring vehicles. The development of safe autonomous vehicles (AVs) poses a challenging task as it requires algorithms that can make real-time decisions in unpredictable circumstances. Reinforcement learning (RL) presents a promising approach for AV control, as it utilizes trial and error to enable optimal decision-making. However, traditional RL algorithms are unsuitable for safety-critical applications, as they may explore unsafe actions, potentially resulting in accidents. Safe reinforcement learning (SRL) algorithms have been developed to address this issue, prioritizing safe and reliable decisions. These algorithms incorporate constraints to prevent unsafe actions or utilize techniques to estimate action risk and avoid actions deemed excessively risky. Despite computational challenges, SRL holds significant promise for AV control, and is likely to play a crucial role in developing safe and reliable systems. SRL methods are critical for the general adoption of autonomous vehicles by guaranteeing their safety and reliability. These algorithms utilize methods like uncertainty and risk estimation along with penalty functions, to avoid excessively risky actions and have the potential to significantly reduce accidents and build public trust in autonomous driving. However, there are challenges that need to be addressed, such as the dynamic nature of real-world traffic, high computational costs, and the diversity of road design; and these varying conditions make the designing, testing, and validating of SRL algorithms difficult. Despite these challenges, SRL presents a promising solution, through integrating new sensing technologies and machine learning techniques, to develop safe, efficient, and environmentally friendly transportation systems.

2026, IFAC Journal of Systems and Control  Show abstract This paper develops a general Lyapunov-based framework for state-feedback control of nonlinear discrete-time systems, where the controller is designed to offer formal assurance of the monotonic decrease of a quadratic Lyapunov function while explicitly accounting for actuator saturation (input constraints). The framework is first presented in a general setting, emphasizing stability conditions under practical limits, and then applied to a case study in autonomous driving. The core difficulty lies in analytically deriving the feedback gains to satisfy both the Hurwitz stability criteria and desired transient (damping) specifications, while maintaining a low-complexity structure. Using a simplified vehicle model, two controllers are compared: a basic proportional feedback law and a Lyapunov-stable controller (LSC) that explicitly incorporates lateral deviation into the control policy. Both controllers are evaluated on real-world driving trajectories from the comma2k19 dataset. Simulation results demonstrate that the LSC significantly improves lane-keeping performance and accelerates convergence to the equilibrium compared to the baseline controller. The novelty of this work lies in bridging Lyapunov stability analysis with practical control evaluation on real driving data, offering a systematic approach to controller design.

## Abstract

Legged robots are ideal for navigating unstructured terrain. Unlike wheeled robot platforms, legged robots maintain mobility over rocks, slopes, and uneven surfaces. However, motion planning in such environments remains challenging. The robot must handle unstable ground, limited sensing, and complex body dynamics. Classical control methods often fail to adapt when terrain and friction change unexpectedly. This paper presents an adaptive locomotion framework for quadrupedal robots. The controller is trained entirely in simulation using deep reinforcement learning (DRL). The DRL is trained using proximal policy optimization (PPO) method. During training, the robot observes joint states, body attitude, and local terrain height information. Training follows a curriculum mechanism. The robot starts on flat terrain. The difficulty gradually increases with slopes, height noise, rough surfaces, and friction variation. The reward function encourages forward progress, stability, low foot slip, and energy-efficient motion. Training occurs in Webots with wide domain randomization ranges. Policies learn to select footholds, regulate body attitude, and minimize slip without explicit terrain labels or gait scripts. Several behaviors emerge through learning. These include wider stance on slopes, increased step height on rocks, and hip abduction for balance recovery. To ensure robustness, we apply a multi-step validation process. These include cross-simulator evaluation, domain randomization Monte Carlo tests, physics consistency tests and adversarial disturbances. The controller achieves 94.6% success in Webots and 91.2% in PyBullet without retraining. It recovers from external pushes within 1.6 seconds. Results confirm that the proposed method learns stable, energy-efficient walking with minimal foot slippage across friction coefficients $\mu = 0.1 t o 1.0$. This capability supports deployment in search-and-rescue, off-road mobility, and exploration tasks in unknown terrain.

## Introduction

Legged robots are nowadays being considered as an important solution for moving in complex and unstructured terrains. From disaster affected areas to very remote extraterrestrial surface, the requirement of autonomous mobility in environment which are not suitable for wheeled or tracked vehicles is increasing day by day. As compared to wheeled robots, legged robots, specially quadruped robots, are having more adaptability in environments having irregular geometry, debris, slopes and gaps. This inspiration taken from biological animals, mainly mammals like dogs and mountain goats, is not only giving better terrain coverage but also providing improved maneuverability, stability and access to areas which were not reachable earlier.

Despite these advantages, motion planning for legged robots remains one of the most challenging problem in the field of robotics. The main difficulty lies in the dynamic interaction between the mechanical structure of the robot and the unpredictable terrain which it has to traverse. Such environments are often presenting discontinuous and unstable surfaces, due to which the robot is required to continuously adjust its center of mass, joint angles and foot placement in real time. The traditional motion planning approaches, which are mostly based on classical control theory or model predictive control (MPC), are ill-suited for these fast changing situations. These methods rely heavily on precise environment models and deterministic behaviors, which falter in the face of incomplete sensing, dynamic ground conditions, and unforeseen disturbances.

In response to these limitations, the researchers are increasingly turning towards learning based methods, specially deep reinforcement learning (DRL), as a viable alternative for generating adaptive locomotion policies. DRL enables the robots to learn control strategies directly by interacting with the environment, without having requirement of explicit modeling of terrain dynamics. Among different DRL algorithms, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) have gained prominence due to its robustness, sample efficiency and ability to handle continuous control tasks with high-dimensional state and action spaces.However, direct training of such complex behaviors in unstructured terrains often results in unstable policy or poor generalization performance. At this stage, curriculum learning becomes very much critical.

Inspired from the way how humans and animals are acquiring complex skills, curriculum learning is structuring the learning process by first starting with simple tasks and then gradually increasing the difficulty level. In the context of locomotion, this means training begins on flat, predictable terrain and gradually introduces complexity such as slopes, friction variation, and rough topography. This step by step learning process is not only helping to stabilize the training but also encouraging the eemergence of generalizable locomotion strategies.By the time the agent is exposed to complex terrain, it has already mastered the fundamental principles of gait stability and energy-efficient movement.

In this paper, we present a novel adaptive motion planning framework for quadrupedal robots that uses DRL with curriculum learning to develop robust and efficient locomotor behavior. The proposed system is trained using a custom simulation environment in Webots. The simulation allows systematic generation of different terrain types. These include variations in friction coefficients, surface slopes, and rocky layers. The robot sensory inputs includes both proprioceptive data and terrain related feedback. Proprioceptive information consists of joint position, joint velocity, and applied torque. Terrain feedback is obtained from simulated exteroceptive sensors, which allows the robot to perceive ground conditions and respond to them in real time during locomotion.

Our approach emphasises minimal reliance on pre programmed movements. It also avoids manually tuned control heuristics. Instead of this, the learning process is mostly autonomous and guided by a carefully crafted reward function. The reward function encourages stability. It supports smoother gait transitions. It also promotes forward progression and lower energy usage during motion. Notably, the robot learns adaptive foot placement over time. It compensates for uneven terrain conditions. At the same time, it maintains overall balance and motion efficiency during locomotion tasks.

We evaluate our framework using both quantitative metrics and qualitative analysis. Results from simulated trials demonstrate the effectiveness of the learned policies in navigating challenging terrains, including sloped, low-friction, and rocky environments. The system shows resilience to sensor noise and continues to exhibit stable behavior even when confronted with terrain configurations not encountered during training. Additionally, an ablation study highlights the contribution of each component–DRL, curriculum structure, and reward shaping–to the overall performance of the system. In summary, our contributions are as follows:

*   We introduce a DRL-based motion planning system for quadrupedal (four legged) robots that learns stable locomotion in unstructured terrain through curriculum learning.

*   We develop a versatile simulation environment with procedurally generated terrains and integrated sensor noise modeling to simulate real-world challenges.

*   We design a multi-component reward function that facilitates the emergence of energy-efficient and adaptive gaits.

*   We demonstrate that the learned policies generalize well across different terrains and maintain robust performance under sensor uncertainty.

*   We validate robust cross-simulator generalization by transferring learned control policies from Webots to PyBullet without re-tuning/re-taining. Webots and PyBullet, both are simulation platform.

*   A rigorous five-stage validation process including cross-simulator tests, domain-randomization Monte-Carlo runs, physics-consistency checks, and adversarial-disturbance testing.

The findings of this research have significant implications for real-world applications such as search and rescue, planetary exploration, and off-road logistics. By enabling robots to dynamically adapt to unpredictable ground conditions, this research brings us closer to deploying fully autonomous walking/legged robots capable of operating in environments where human access is limited, unsafe, or risky.

## Related work

The development of autonomous locomotion strategies for legged robots has remained as a long standing objective in the field of robotics. Over the years, researchers have explored different types of control approaches, ranging from rule based motion planning methods to more recent learning based techniques. This section is reviewing the related prior works in important areas such as classical planning, model based control, reinforcement learning, curriculum learning and terrain simulation. It also highlights the limitations present in existing approaches and explains how the proposed method is contributing towards advancement of the state of the art.

### Classical motion planning and model-based control

Traditional approaches for robot locomotion are mostly depending on deterministic control principles which are derived from physical models of the robot and its environment. Algorithms such as A* (star) and Rapidly Exploring Random Trees (RRT) are adapted for foot based locomotion by calculating possible foot positions and body trajectories. These algorithms are working well in known or structured terrain situations. However, they are often failing in dynamic and uncertain environments. This is mainly due to their reliance on precise terrain maps and also because of high computational complexity[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR1 "Zhang, Q., Hu, S., Duan, J., Qin, J. & Zhou, Y. A sac-bi-rrt two-layer real-time motion planning approach for robot assembly tasks in unstructured environments, in Actuators, MDPI, 14, 59. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/act14020059
                  
                 (2025)."),[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR2 "Li, Z., Chen, Y., Zhang, Z., Zhong, H. & Wang, Y. Frt*: fast reactive tree for mobile robot replanning in unknown dynamic environments. Robotic Intelligence and Automation 45, 173–186. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1108/RIA-10-2024-0211
                  
                 (2025).").

Model based controllers, including Zero Moment Point (ZMP) and Model Predictive Control (MPC), are providing dynamic stability by continuously optimizing the pose of the robot and its center of mass. These control methods are widely used in bipedal and quadrupedal robotic platforms such as ASIMO and MIT Cheetah. However, such approaches require very accurate dynamic models of the robot system. They are also highly sensitive to modeling errors, sensor noise and unexpected external disturbances, which makes them more brittle and less reliable in real world scenarios[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR3 "Yang, T., Tong, Y. & Zhang, Z. Flexible model predictive control for bounded gait generation in humanoid robots. Biomimetics 10, 30. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/biomimetics10010030
                  
                 (2025)."),[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR4 "Gu, Z., et al. Humanoid locomotion and manipulation: Current progress and challenges in control, planning, and learning, arXiv preprint 
                  arXiv:2501.02116
                  
                 (2025). 
                  https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2501.02116
                  
                .").

### Deep reinforcement learning for locomotion

Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) allows robotic agents to learn locomotion and control policies through trial and error interaction with the environment. In contrast to traditional model based approaches, DRL does not require explicitly defined physical models of the robot or surroundings. Due to this advantage, DRL has achieved major success in simulation environments, where agents are able to learn complex behaviors such as walking, running and obstacle avoidance[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR5 "Honelign, L., Abebe, Y., Tullu, A. & Jung, S. Deep reinforcement learning-based enhancement of robotic arm target-reaching performance, in Actuators, MDPI, 14, 165. 
                  https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0825/14/4/165
                  
                .(2025)."),[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR6 "Gao, J. et al. Reinforcement learning decision-making for autonomous vehicles based on semantic segmentation. Applied Sciences 15, 1323. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/app15031323
                  
                 (2025).").

DRL has been widely applied in OpenAI Gym environments such as HalfCheetah, Ant and Walker2D, and more recently in MuJoCo based locomotion benchmarks developed by Google DeepMind. These works demonstrate that DRL agents are capable of learning complex and human like gait patterns. However, many early DRL based approaches were limited mainly to flat simulated terrains and showed poor generalization in real world scenarios. This is largely due to sensor uncertainty and environmental variability[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR7 "Bochem, S., Gonzalez-Sanchez, E., Bicker, Y. & Fadini, G. Improving generalization of robot locomotion policies via sharpness-aware reinforcement learning, arXiv preprint 
                  arXiv:2411.19732
                  
                 (2024)."),[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR8 "Ulloa, C. C., Zaramalilea, M., Orbea, D., Del Cerro, J. & Barrientos, A.Probabilistic terrain analysis using semantic criteria for legged robot locomotion, in 2024 7th Iberian Robotics Conference (ROBOT), 1–6 (IEEE, 2024), 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/ROBOT61475.2024.10796929
                  
                .").

In real world robotics applications, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has been applied to legged robotic platforms such as ANYmal and Spot (from Boston Dynamics), allowing them to learn locomotion behaviors like walking and stair climbing. However, in most practical deployments, hybrid control approaches are commonly used, where DRL is combined with model based controllers or additional safety mechanisms in order to ensure stability and robustness of the system. These robotic systems are usually restricted to controlled operating environments,since achieving generalization across unstructured terrain remains a major challenge due to variable ground conditions and sensor noise[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR1 "Zhang, Q., Hu, S., Duan, J., Qin, J. & Zhou, Y. A sac-bi-rrt two-layer real-time motion planning approach for robot assembly tasks in unstructured environments, in Actuators, MDPI, 14, 59. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/act14020059
                  
                 (2025).").

### Curriculum learning in robotics

Curriculum learning is inspired from cognitive science and it suggests that learning becomes more effective when tasks are presented in a gradual manner, from easy to more difficult levels. In robotics domain, this principle has been successfully applied to stabilize deep reinforcement learning (DRL) training process, improve convergence, and enhance generalization across different environments[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR9 "Fu, W., et al. Areal: A large-scale asynchronous reinforcement learning system for language reasoning, arXiv preprint 
                  arXiv:2505.24298
                  
                 (2025). ").

Several recent studies have applied curriculum learning techniques to enhance locomotion performance in robotic system. For instance[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR10 "Yu, W., Liu, C. K. & Turk, G. Policy transfer with strategy optimization, arXiv preprint 
                  arXiv:1810.05751
                  
                . (2018)."), showed improved control policies by gradually increasing the terrain complexity during the training process. Various terrain interpolation strategies, starting from flat surface and moving towards more rugged terrain, together with task decomposition methods such as learning to stand before walking, have been shown to stabilize the training process and promote better policy generalization. In a similar way[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR11 "Tidd, B., Hudson, N. & Cosgun, A. Guided curriculum learning for walking over complex terrain, arXiv preprint 
                  arXiv:2010.03848
                  
                . (2020)."), proposed a multi-stage curriculum learning approach, where the learning agents were progressively exposed to different terrain conditions and external disturbances, which resulted in significant improvement in bipedal walking performance.

Despite its benefits, curriculum learning is still not commonly adopted as a standard component in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) based locomotion frameworks. In this work, we advance the existing research by integrating a finely staged terrain curriculum directly into the DRL training pipeline. This allows the learning agent to first master basic locomotion skills before moving towards more complex terrains involving friction variation, sensor noise and instability. Such a training strategy helps to address key limitations related to DRL generalization in unstructured environments[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR12 "Ha, S., et al. Learning-based legged locomotion: State of the art and future perspectives, The International Journal of Robotics Research 02783649241312698. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/02783649241312698
                  
                 (2024).").

### Reward design for locomotion tasks

The performance of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) in locomotion tasks depends heavily on the design of the reward function. Common reward components include balance maintenance, energy minimization, target velocity tracking and penalization of undesired behaviors such as foot slippage. However, reward shaping is mostly empirical in nature, and poorly designed reward functions can result in unstable or sub optimal behaviors. Recent research highlights the need for adaptive and task aware reward mechanisms to improve training stability and real world transfer capability[13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR13 "Nasiri, R., Dinovitzer, H., Manohara, N. & Arami, A. Coordinated human-exoskeleton locomotion emerges from regulating virtual energy. PloS one 20, e0292334. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0292334
                  
                 (2025).").

Recent studies show that combining multiple reward parameters, such as forward velocity, gait symmetry, torque efficiency and terrain adaptability, leads to more natural and stable locomotion. In this work, we design a composite reward function that assists smooth transitions, robust stance behavior, energy efficient movement and reliable terrain negotiation. This reward design builds upon existing approaches for optimizing quadruped gait generation[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR14 "Sulpice, L., Owaki, D. & Hayashibe, M. Footstep reward for energy-efficient quadruped gait generation and transition through deep reinforcement learning. Advanced Robotics 39, 71–78. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1080/01691864.2024.2442718
                  
                 (2025).").

### Simulated terrain and domain randomization

Training robots in diverse terrain environments is essential for achieving adaptable locomotion performance. Simulation platforms such as MuJoCo, PyBullet, Isaac Gym and Gazebo are widely used to model complex terrain types including hills, stairs and deformable surfaces. Procedural terrain generation has become an effective method to expose DRL agents to varied and unpredictable conditions during training, thereby improving their robustness and generalization capability[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR15 "Yu, S., Perera, N., Marew, D. & Kim, D. Learning generic and dynamic locomotion of humanoids across discrete terrains, in 2024 IEEE-RAS 23rd International Conference on Humanoid Robots (Humanoids), 1048–1055. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/Humanoids58906.2024.10769916
                  
                 (IEEE, 2024)."),[16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR16 "Cano, L., Tardioli, D. & Mosteo, A. R. Procedural generation of tunnel networks for unsupervised training and testing in underground applications, in 2024 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS), 4608–4615. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/IROS58592.2024.10801552
                  
                 (IEEE, 2024).").

In parallel, domain randomization techniques, where physical and environmental parameters such as friction, mass and sensor noise are varied during simulation, have been shown to improve sim to real transfer capability of learned policies[17](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR17 "Nong, Y. Meta-domain adaptive transfer (mdat) learning for rapid adaptation in simulated robotic tasks. 
                  https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-5806840/v1
                  
                 (2025)."). Although the current work is focused on simulation based validation, environmental variations such as slope and surface noise are incorporated to prepare the policy for broader generalization and future real world deployment.

While significant progress has been achieved in DRL based locomotion, many challenges still remain in achieving reliable performance on unstructured terrain. Classical control approaches lack adaptability, while many DRL based methods struggle to scale to real world conditions[18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR18 "Zhang, Y., Zeng, J., Sun, H., Sun, H. & Hashimoto, K. Dual-layer reinforcement learning for quadruped robot locomotion and speed control in complex environments. Applied Sciences 14, 8697. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/app14198697
                  
                 (2024)."). The proposed approach addresses these challenges by integrating curriculum learning, procedural terrain generation and composite reward shaping within a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) based DRL framework. This combination facilitates efficient and autonomous navigation for quadrupedal robots in complex environments.

### Quadrupedal robot model

This robot is a fully simulated quadruped platform designed for use in the Webots robotics simulator. It is designed to support research and development in leg movement, perception, and control. With four articulated legs and a modular design, it performs well in a variety of environments, from flat indoor surfaces to rough outdoor terrain.

*   Structure

    *   The robot has a central rectangular body with a smooth blue finish and slightly rounded corners.

    *   The body houses all virtual electronics, computing, and sensors in the simulation.

*   Leg configuration

    *   The robot features four legs, each with three degrees of freedom (3-DOF).

        *   $*$ Hip joint – for forward/backward swing.

        *   $*$ Thigh joint – to lift or lower the leg.

        *   $*$ Knee joint – for bending at the lower leg.

    *   With three actuated joints per leg, the robot has a total of 12 actuated joints.

    *   Each joint is represented in Webots using _HingeJoint_, driven by _RotationalMotor_ components and measured via _PositionSensor_ feedback.

*   Visual Design

    *   Body color: Bright blue for visual clarity.

    *   Joint casings: Distinct yellow, marking articulation points.

    *   Legs:

        *   $*$ Upper segments: Dark gray.

        *   $*$ Lower segments: Bright lime green.

        *   $*$ Feet: Rounded and black for clear contrast and stability.

The quadruped robot is modeled as a 12-DOF system in eq.([3.1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Equ1)):

$$
\textbf{q} = \left[\right. q_{1} , q_{2} , \ldots , q_{12} \left]\right.^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{12}
$$

 (3.1) 

where $q_{i}$ represents the angular position of joint $i$. Each leg has 3 actuated joints: hip abduction/adduction, hip flexion/extension, and knee flexion/extension.

The robot state at time $t$ is defined in eq.([3.2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Equ2)):

$$
s_{t} = \left(\right. \textbf{q}_{t} , \overset{\cdot}{\textbf{q}}_{t} , \textbf{R}_{t} , \textbf{p}_{t} , \textbf{v}_{t} \left.\right)
$$

 (3.2) 

where

*   $\textbf{q}_{t}$: joint angles

*   $\overset{\cdot}{\textbf{q}}_{t}$: joint velocities

*   $\textbf{R}_{t} \in S O \left(\right. 3 \left.\right)$: orientation matrix from the IMU

*   $\textbf{p}_{t} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$: base position

*   $\textbf{v}_{t} \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$: base linear velocity

The robot’s motion obeys the rigid-body dynamics shown in eq.([3.3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Equ3)):

$$
\textbf{M} \left(\right. \textbf{q} \left.\right) \overset{\cdot\cdot}{\textbf{q}} + \textbf{C} \left(\right. \textbf{q} , \overset{\cdot}{\textbf{q}} \left.\right) \overset{\cdot}{\textbf{q}} + \textbf{g} \left(\right. \textbf{q} \left.\right) = \tau \tau + \textbf{J}^{\top} \left(\right. \textbf{q} \left.\right) \textbf{f}_{\text{ext}}
$$

 (3.3) 

where

*   $\textbf{M} \left(\right. \textbf{q} \left.\right)$: mass matrix

*   $\textbf{C} \left(\right. \textbf{q} , \overset{\cdot}{\textbf{q}} \left.\right)$: Coriolis and centrifugal terms

*   $\textbf{g} \left(\right. \textbf{q} \left.\right)$: gravitational torque

*   $\tau \tau$: actuator torques

*   $\textbf{J} \left(\right. \textbf{q} \left.\right)$: Jacobian matrix

*   $\textbf{f}_{\text{ext}}$: external contact forces from terrain contact

### Terrain and environment model

The terrain is developed in Webots[19](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR19 "Cyberbotics Ltd., cyberbotics/webots: Webots robot simulator, 
                  https://github.com/cyberbotics/webots
                  
                , (2025). Accessed July 2025."), which provides a physics engine capable of simulating real-world forces and collisions. Terrain surfaces are procedurally generated to introduce variability in locomotion tasks. Typical terrain features include:

*   Sloped surfaces,

*   Irregular rocks and bumps,

*   Flat patches and narrow paths,

*   Uneven or low-friction (slippery) areas.

These terrains vary in height, surface friction, and texture. During training, the environment parameters are randomized to promote generalization across unseen conditions. Webots also enables real-time visualization, robot–terrain interactions, and performance monitoring.

The ground height is modeled as a continuous map as defined in eq.([3.4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Equ4)):

$$
h \left(\right. x , y \left.\right) : \mathbb{R}^{2} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}
$$

 (3.4) 

such that the contact height at each foot position $\left(\right. x_{j} , y_{j} \left.\right)$ is computed by eq.([3.5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Equ5)):

$$
h_{j} = h \left(\right. x_{j} , y_{j} \left.\right)
$$

 (3.5) 

Different terrain profiles are generated using the following mechanisms:

*   Gaussian noise fields to emulate natural uneven ground,

*   Piecewise planar functions for ramps and stair surfaces,

*   Spatially varying friction coefficients $\mu_{j} \in \left[\right. 0.1 , 1.0 \left]\right.$ at each contact point.

#### Friction coefficient justification

The chosen interval [0.1,1.0] reflects realistic surface conditions observed in both natural and artificial (simulated) environments. Representative values from the literature[20](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR20 "Shi, H., et al. Terrain-aware quadrupedal locomotion via reinforcement learning, arXiv preprint 
                  arXiv:2310.04675
                  
                . (2023)."),[21](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR21 "Gangapurwala, S., Geisert, M., Orsolino, R., Fallon, M. & Havoutis, I. Rloc: Terrain-aware legged locomotion using reinforcement learning and optimal control. IEEE Transactions on Robotics 38, 2908–2927. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/TRO.2022.3172469
                  
                 (2022).") are shown in Table[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Tab1).

**Table 1 Typical coefficients of friction for common surfaces.**

[Full size table](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7/tables/1)

Thus, the interval captures the majority of terrains relevant to mobile robotics, ranging from low-friction surfaces that cause slippage to high-friction conditions that provide secure footholds. While values above 1.0 may occur in special cases (e.g., climbing shoes or adhesive rubber), they are not typical for the ground locomotion tasks considered here.

#### Friction force approximation

The friction force at foot _j_ is modeled as the tangential component of the ground reaction force (GRF). The friction approximation is expressed in eq.([3.6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Equ6)):

$$
\textbf{f}_{\text{fric} , j} = - \mu_{j} f_{j}^{n} \frac{\textbf{v}_{j}^{t}}{\parallel \textbf{v}_{j}^{t} \parallel + \epsilon}
$$

 (3.6) 

where

*   $\mu_{j}$ is the coefficient of friction at foot _j_,

*   $f_{j}^{n} \approx m_{j} g$ is the normal force (approximated by the effective mass supported by the foot),

*   $\textbf{v}_{j}^{t}$ is the tangential velocity of the foot at contact,

*   $\epsilon$ is a small regularization term to avoid division by zero.

The direction of friction is opposite to tangential slip velocity. The total GRF (Ground Reaction Force) at foot $j$ is given in eq.([3.7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Equ7)):

$$
\textbf{F}_{j} = f_{j}^{n} \hat{\mathbf{n}} + \textbf{f}_{\text{fric} , j}
$$

 (3.7) 

where $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the terrain surface normal at the contact point.

To ensure physical consistency, friction must satisfy the classical friction cone constraint shown in eq.([3.8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Equ8)):

$$
\parallel \textbf{f}_{\text{fric} , j} \parallel \leq \mu_{j} f_{j}^{n}
$$

 (3.8) 

which guarantees that the total GRF remains within feasible contact forces for stable locomotion.

### Control structure

The control architecture is hierarchical with two layers.

#### Low-level joint controller

Each joint is actuated using a Proportional–Derivative (PD) controller, expressed in eq.([3.9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Equ9)):

$$
\tau_{i} = K_{p , i} \left(\right. q_{i}^{\text{des}} - q_{i} \left.\right) + K_{d , i} \left(\right. \overset{\cdot}{q}_{i}^{\text{des}} - \overset{\cdot}{q}_{i} \left.\right)
$$

 (3.9) 

where $q_{i}^{\text{des}}$ is the desired joint angle provided by the high-level policy.

**PD Gain Selection:**

The PD gains are initially selected via classical second-order system tuning assumptions, shown in eq.([3.10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Equ10)):

$$
K_{p} = \omega_{n}^{2} I , K_{d} = 2 \zeta \omega_{n} I
$$

 (3.10) 

where $\omega_{n}$ is the natural frequency, $\zeta$ is the damping ratio, and $I$ is the joint inertia. These baseline gains are then refined via simulation tuning to ensure stable yet responsive tracking without excessive torque demand, consistent with modern practices in legged robotics[22](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR22 "Kolathaya, S. Local stability of pd controlled bipedal walking robots. Automatica 114, 108841. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.automatica.2020.108841
                  
                 (2020)."),[23](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR23 "Liang, Y., Yin, F., Peng, Z., Zhao, Y. & Yan, W. Hierarchical optimization-based hybrid whole-body control for wheel-legged robots, in International Conference on Intelligent Robotics and Applications, 62–73. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-96-0798-3_6
                  
                 (Springer, 2024).").

**Table 2 PD gains used for different joint types in the experimental setup.**

[Full size table](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7/tables/2)

The final PD gains used for each joint type are listed in Table[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Tab2). The gains remain fixed during both training and deployment phases. The use of fixed PD control at the joint level follows recent hierarchical locomotion approaches employing PD or impedance modules for reliable low-level tracking[24](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR24 "Sun, G., Shafiee, M., Li, P., Bellegarda, G., Ijspeert, A. & Sartoretti, G. Learning-based hierarchical control: Emulating the central nervous system for bio-inspired legged robot locomotion, in 2024 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS), 13938–13945.
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/IROS58592.2024.10801412
                  
                 (IEEE, 2024)."),[25](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR25 "Wang, H. et al. Whole-body constrained learning for legged locomotion via hierarchical optimization. IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/LRA.2025.3577526
                  
                 (2025)."),[26](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR26 "Huang, X., et al. Hilma-res: A general hierarchical framework via residual rl for combining quadrupedal locomotion and manipulation, in 2024 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS), 9050–9057. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/IROS58592.2024.10802517
                  
                 (IEEE, 2024).").

#### High-level policy controller

The high-level controller outputs either joint targets (eq.([3.11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Equ11))) or desired foot positions (eq.([3.12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Equ12))):

$$
\textbf{a}_{t} = \left[\right. q_{1}^{\text{des}} , \ldots , q_{12}^{\text{des}} \left]\right.
$$

 (3.11) 

$$
\textbf{f}_{j}^{\text{des}} = \left[\right. x_{j}^{\text{des}} , y_{j}^{\text{des}} , z_{j}^{\text{des}} \left]\right. , j \in \left{\right. 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 \left.\right}
$$

 (3.12) 

If desired foot positions are provided, joint angles are obtained via inverse kinematics (IK) by solving eq.([3.13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Equ13)):

$$
\underset{\textbf{q}_{j}}{min} \parallel \textbf{f}_{j} \left(\right. \textbf{q}_{j} \left.\right) - \textbf{f}_{j}^{\text{des}} \parallel^{2}
$$

 (3.13) 

subject to joint limits in eq.([3.14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Equ14)):

$$
\textbf{q}_{j}^{min} \leq \textbf{q}_{j} \leq \textbf{q}_{j}^{max}
$$

 (3.14) 

This hierarchical structure aligns with current state-of-the-art locomotion and loco-manipulation systems[27](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#ref-CR27 "Xu, Z., Raj, A. H., Xiao, X. & Stone, P. Dexterous legged locomotion in confined 3d spaces with reinforcement learning, in 2024 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA),  11474–11480. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/ICRA57147.2024.10610668
                  
                 (IEEE, 2024).").

#### Control frequencies

The high-level policy outputs actions at 10 Hz (every 100 ms), which is sufficient for stable locomotion. The low-level PD loop runs at 100 Hz, matching the simulator timestep. While a 10 Hz policy rate is used throughout this study, the simulator and control architecture can technically support action updates up to 100 Hz, which is the maximum limit imposed by the Webots (simulator) timestep (10 milliseconds). This provides flexibility for future work to explore higher-frequency policies.

### Sensor and state representation

The robot is equipped with simulated sensors. They are listed below:

*   IMU: provides orientation $\textbf{R} \in S O \left(\right. 3 \left.\right)$ and angular velocity

*   Joint encoders: measure $\textbf{q} , \overset{\cdot}{\textbf{q}}$

*   Depth camera: outputs a local terrain heightmap $\textbf{H} \in \mathbb{R}^{w \times h}$

The full robot state at time $t$ is defined in eq.([3.15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Equ15)):

$$
s_{t} = \left[\right. \textbf{q} , \overset{\cdot}{\textbf{q}} , \textbf{R} , \textbf{v} , \textbf{f}_{\text{contact}} , \text{flatten} \left(\right. \textbf{H} \left.\right) \left]\right.
$$

 (3.15) 

where $\textbf{f}_{\text{contact}}$ denotes binary foot contact indicators.

### Terrain-adaptive gait strategy

To improve robustness, a terrain-aware gating mechanism can be used. A convolutional neural network $\phi \left(\right. \textbf{H} \left.\right)$ processes the heightmap and outputs a terrain class, as defined in eq.([3.16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Equ16)):

$$
\phi \left(\right. \textbf{H} \left.\right) \rightarrow \text{Terrain Type} \in \left{\right. \text{flat} , \text{slope} , \text{rocky} , \text{slippery} \left.\right}
$$

 (3.16) 

The terrain label modulates gait selection to enhance stability and traction. For example:

*   Flat terrain $\rightarrow$ trot

*   Rocky terrain $\rightarrow$ crawl

*   Slope $\rightarrow$ low-CoM climbing posture

## Learning framework

This section explains the reinforcement learning setup used to train the quadruped robot in Webots. It includes the learning algorithm, observation and action spaces, reward design, and curriculum learning strategy.

### Reinforcement learning formulation

The locomotion problem is modeled as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). The MDP is defined by the tuple in eq.([4.1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Equ17)):

$$
\mathcal{M} = \left(\right. \mathcal{S} , \mathcal{A} , \mathcal{P} , r , \gamma \left.\right)
$$

 (4.1) 

Where

*   $\mathcal{S}$ is the state (observation) space–sensor readings including joint states, body orientation, velocity, and local terrain features.

*   $\mathcal{A}$ is the action space, defined as high-level joint or foot position targets tracked by the low-level PD controller (see Sect. “Control structure”). The PD controller subsequently generates the motor torques applied in simulation.

*   $\mathcal{P} \left(\right. s^{'} \left|\right. s , a \left.\right)$ is the state transition probability – governed by the physics engine of the simulator.

*   $r : \mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{A} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is the reward function providing scalar feedback.

*   $\gamma \in \left[\right. 0 , 1 \left]\right.$ is the discount factor– set to 0.99 for long-horizon stability.

The objective is to find a policy $\pi_{\theta} \left(\right. a \mid s \left.\right)$, parameterized by $\theta$, that maximizes the expected return defined in eq.([4.2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Equ18)):

$$
J \left(\right. \theta \left.\right) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}} \left[\right. \sum_{t = 0}^{T} \gamma^{t} r \left(\right. s_{t} , a_{t} \left.\right) \left]\right.
$$

 (4.2) 

We use Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), optimizing the clipped surrogate objective. PPO is well-suited for continuous control tasks and has been successfully applied in robotics applications due to its stability and ease of implementation. PPO maximizes a clipped surrogate objective shown in eq.([4.3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Equ19)):

$$
L^{\text{CLIP}} \left(\right. \theta \left.\right) = \mathbb{E}_{t} \left[\right. min \left(\right. r_{t} \left(\right. \theta \left.\right) \hat{A}_{t} , \text{clip} \left(\right. r_{t} \left(\right. \theta \left.\right) , 1 - \epsilon , 1 + \epsilon \left.\right) \hat{A}_{t} \left.\right) \left]\right.
$$

 (4.3) 

where $r_{t} \left(\right. \theta \left.\right) = \frac{\pi_{\theta} \left(\right. a_{t} \mid s_{t} \left.\right)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}} \left(\right. a_{t} \mid s_{t} \left.\right)}$ is the policy ratio, $\hat{A}_{t}$ is the advantage estimate, and $\epsilon = 0.2$ is the clipping parameter. PPO is particularly effective in stabilizing learning for legged locomotion tasks.

### Observation space

The observation vector at time $t$ is defined in eq.([4.4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-34956-7#Equ20)):

$$
s_{t} = \left[\right. \textbf{q} , \overset{\cdot}{\textbf{q}} , \textbf{R} , \textbf{v} , \textbf{f}_{c} , \textbf{h} \left]\right.
$$

 (4.4) 

where $s_{t} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ represents the full state observation used by the policy.

The observation components are:

*   $\textbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^{12}$: joint angles (12 joints)

*   $\overset{\cdot}{\textbf{q}} \in \mathbb{R}^{12}$

This is a scientific research article published in *Scientific Reports* (Volume 16, Article 4669, 2026) by Mohammad Salah uddin, presenting an adaptive motion planning framework for quadrupedal (legged) robots navigating unstructured terrain using deep reinforcement learning (DRL) with curriculum learning.

**Key Methodology:**
- The controller is trained entirely in simulation using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) within the Webots simulator.
- Training follows a curriculum mechanism: starting on flat terrain, then gradually increasing difficulty with slopes, height noise, rough surfaces, and friction variation.
- The robot observes joint states, body attitude, and local terrain height information.
- The reward function encourages forward progress, stability, low foot slip, and energy-efficient motion.
- Domain randomization is applied to physical/environmental parameters for robustness.

**Robot Architecture:**
- A 12-DOF quadruped robot with three actuated joints per leg (hip, thigh, knee).
- Hierarchical control: high-level policy outputs actions at 10 Hz, low-level PD control loop runs at 100 Hz.
- Sensors include IMU, joint encoders, and depth camera for terrain height mapping.

**Key Results:**
- The controller achieves 94.6% success rate in Webots and 91.2% in PyBullet without retraining (cross-simulator generalization).
- Recovers from external pushes within 1.6 seconds.
- Stable walking across friction coefficients μ = 0.1 to 1.0.
- Learned behaviors include wider stance on slopes, increased step height on rocks, and hip abduction for balance recovery.
- Validation includes multi-step process: cross-simulator evaluation, domain randomization Monte Carlo tests, physics consistency tests, and adversarial disturbances.

**Contributions:**
1. DRL-based motion planning with curriculum learning for quadruped locomotion.
2. Versatile simulation environment with procedurally generated terrains and sensor noise.
3. Multi-component reward function for energy-efficient and adaptive gaits.
4. Demonstrated policy generalization across different terrains.
5. Cross-simulator validation from Webots to PyBullet.
6. Rigorous five-stage validation process.

The research has implications for search-and-rescue, off-road mobility, planetary exploration, and exploration tasks in unknown terrain.

## Abstract

Bipedal robots are gaining global recognition due to their potential applications and the rapid advancements in artificial intelligence, particularly through deep reinforcement learning (DRL). While DRL has significantly advanced bipedal locomotion, the development of a unified framework capable of handling a wide range of tasks remains an ongoing challenge. This survey systematically categorises, compares, and analyses existing DRL frameworks for bipedal locomotion, organising them into end-to-end and hierarchical control schemes. End-to-end frameworks are evaluated based on their learning approaches, whereas hierarchical frameworks are examined in terms of their layered structures that integrate learning-based and traditional model-based methods. We provide a detailed evaluation of the composition, strengths, limitations, and capabilities of each framework. Furthermore, this survey identifies key research gaps and proposes future directions aimed at creating a more integrated and efficient unified framework for bipedal locomotion, with broad applicability in real-world environments.

## 1 Introduction

Humans navigate complex environments and perform diverse locomotion tasks with remarkable efficiency using only two legs. Bipedal robots, which closely mimic the human form, possess distinct advantages over wheeled or tracked alternatives, particularly when traversing uneven and challenging terrains. Furthermore, bipedal humanoid robots are specifically designed to operate in human-centric environments, enabling seamless interaction with tools and infrastructure intended for human use. This makes them highly adaptable to a wide range of tasks in such settings.

As a result, bipedal robots hold significant potential for real-world applications (Tong et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11451-z#ref-CR112 "Tong Y, Liu H, Zhang Z (2024) Advancements in humanoid robots: A comprehensive review and future prospects. IEEE/CAA J Autom Sin 11:301–328")). While model-based approaches offer rapid convergence and predictive capabilities, they often struggle in dynamically complex and uncertain environments where adaptability is essential.

Reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods, particularly deep reinforcement learning (DRL), are effective in optimising robot control policies through direct interaction with the environment (Khan et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11451-z#ref-CR55 "Khan MA-M, Khan MRJ, Tooshil A, Sikder N, Mahmud MAP, Kouzani AZ, Nahid A-A (2020) A systematic review on reinforcement learning-based robotics within the last decade. IEEE Access 8:176598–176623. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2020.3027152
                  
                ")), which provides a distinct advantage. Unlike model-based approaches, which rely on predefined dynamics and may fail under unforeseen conditions, DRL enables robots to autonomously discover control strategies through trial and error, achieving greater adaptability and robustness in diverse environments. In addition, hybrid methods that combine model-based and learning-based techniques further enhance planning and control by leveraging the strengths of both paradigms.

Despite these advancements, research in DRL-based locomotion remains highly fragmented, with inconsistencies in training pipelines, reward formulations, observation spaces, and evaluation setups that hinder systematic benchmarking and slow progress towards generalisable locomotion capabilities. Moreover, many methods are tailored to specific morphologies or tasks, offering limited transferability across embodiments and environments.

This fragmentation motivates the following central research questions: _To what extent has current research achieved generalisation and robustness across diverse morphologies, terrains, and locomotion tasks? If full generalisation has not yet been realised, how can existing DRL approaches be organised and extended towards a unified framework that enables such capability in bipedal robots?_ In this context, the present survey seeks to categorise emerging DRL frameworks for bipedal locomotion, identify their key limitations, and outline opportunities for integration and convergence towards unification.

To address these aspects, we first clarify the ultimate goal of robot learning: to develop systems that exhibit generalisation, adaptability, and robustness across diverse morphologies, tasks, and environments. The unified framework is therefore not the final destination but a conceptual scaffold emerging from the consolidation of current DRL research efforts. Its role is to organise fragmented methodologies through shared interfaces, training conventions, and evaluation protocols, thereby promoting steady progress towards the broader goal of generalisable and adaptive robot-learning systems.

Guided by these definitions, this survey examines recent advancements in DRL-based frameworks, categorising control schemes into two primary types: (i) end-to-end and (ii) hierarchical. End-to-end frameworks directly map robot states to joint-level control outputs, while hierarchical frameworks decompose decision-making into multiple layers. In hierarchical systems, a high-level (HL) planner governs navigation and path planning, while a low-level (LL) controller handles fundamental locomotion tasks. The task-level decision-making tier interfaces directly with user commands or predefined tasks, forming a structured approach to robotic control.

Current progress across both end-to-end and hierarchical paradigms indicates that a unified framework for DRL-based bipedal locomotion is still far from being realised. Establishing such a framework is essential for consolidating diverse learning pipelines, standardising evaluation metrics, and enabling transferable locomotion capabilities across different robot morphologies. As locomotion tasks become increasingly complex, ranging from basic stabilisation to dynamic parkour and loco-manipulation, the need for consistent benchmarking has intensified. The DARPA Robotics Challenge exemplified this trend by introducing one of the first large-scale evaluation platforms for bipedal humanoids performing real-world locomotion and manipulation tasks (Atkeson et al. [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10462-025-11451-z#ref-CR4 "Atkeson CG, Babu BPW, Banerjee N, Berenson D, Bove CP, Cui X, DeDonato M, Du R, Feng S, Franklin P, et al (2015) No falls, no resets: Reliable humanoid behavior in the darpa robotics challenge. In: IEEE-RAS 15th International Conference on Humanoid Robot, pp 623–630")), highlighting the importance of robustness and practical deployment.
